subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT DELAYS IN DEALING WITH APPLICATIONS BE REDUCED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I should like to speak on behalf of some of my constituents who have expressed concern about the inordinate amount of time it takes to obtain Canadian citizenship.
I am told that under normal circumstances the Royal Canadian Mounted Police or the Canadian Security Intelligence Service need three months to file an investigation report.
This sounds like a long delay, but in some cases the authorities do need time to do their work. Well, Mr. Speaker, it would seem that of late these delays have been as long as eight months, and this is unacceptable.
For example, Mr. Georges Tymowski wrote to me recently to inform me that, although he signed his application on June 16, 1986, he is still waiting for the results of the security investigation to complete the process. Mr. Ahmad Awale is another applicant who has been waiting for a long time for the completion of the investigation.
This is an unacceptable situation, Mr. Speaker, because it is prejudicial to people who need access to certain Government services such as passports.
I hope the Government is aware of the problem and will take every measure required to redress the situation.

speakerposition: subtopic

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF WESTERN FORESTS SCIENCE CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, almost half the Members in this House represent ridings whose economies are dependent on the forest industry. To a great extent our nation's future is tied to the future of our forests.
Professor Les Reed and others at the University of British Columbia are discussing putting together a new facility called the Western Forests Science Centre.
Such a world-class facility would involve the forest industry, academics, and Government. It would greatly enhance the capability of the UBC forest faculty to teach and to attract the very best post-graduate students and visiting scholars.
More than that, Mr. Speaker, it would give the forest community in British Columbia a tremendous psychological shot in the arm.
And where would the funding for the Western Forests Science Centre come from? The recently imposed export tax, of course. Only 5 per cent of the funds the Province of British Columbia will receive this year alone would be required.
To paraphrase the poet:
I think that I shall never see A poem, lovely as a tree . . .
But more than that, 1 hope there'll be,
A Forest Science Centre, at UBC!

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF NEW EMBASSY IN WASHINGTON-USE OF NON-UNION LABOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as Canada focuses on its relationship with the United States during the visit of President Reagan, I want to draw attention to Canada's use of non-union labour in the construction of the new Canadian Embassy in Washington.
The Embassy is being built by union contractors except for three crafts, one of which is the sheet metal workers, who are

April 3, 1987
being paid substandard wages, with no health or other benefits.
Because many of these workers lack experience and training, there is concern that some of their work will not pass inspection, and that safety and health problems will result.
Since December of last year union officials have tried to meet with our Ambassador to discuss the problem. While the Embassy has agreed in principle to such a meeting, it has never set the time or the place.
I urge the Government to instruct our Ambassador to arrange this meeting in the near future so that the problem can be resolved.
We need to have good relations not only with American officials but also with the American people, including working people.

subsubtopic: CRITICISM OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government's current standing in the polls is no accident.
During the 1984 election campaign the Tories made many promises which they have since broken.
Nowhere is this record more horrendous than in its treatment of the Canadian shipbuilding industry.
In fact the Conservatives have not only broken their promises, they have slashed the shipbuilding industry assistance program, and they have slashed the performance improvement grants just when these programs were most needed.
The situation is even worse for shipyards in Atlantic Canada. In my province there is the Georgetown shipyard. The future of its workers is not solely a provincial responsibility as some would suggest. At a recent meeting the Council of Maritime Premiers expressed their impatience with the federal Government which has turned a blind eye toward Atlantic Canada. I call upon the Government to get off its seat and take some action.

speakerposition: subtopic

subsubtopic: WORK OF CANADIAN AVIATION SAFETY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since its inception in 1984, the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, through its independent investigation of accidents and its recommendations, has done much to advance air safety in Canada.
Canadian aviation activity is very high with 26,000 civil aircraft and 1,300 licensed airports handling annually some 54 million passengers. In 1986 there were 495 aircraft accidents in Canada, 73 of which involved fatalities.
The recent annual report of the board shows a favourable continuing downward trend in the accident rate, but unfortunately accident survivability remains unchanged.
Let us encourage the board in its important work of making air travel in Canada even safer than is presently the case.

subsubtopic: LYELL ISLAND-CONTINUATION OF LOGGING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many Canadians think that a settlement has been reached between the Haida people, the federal Government, and Victoria regarding Lyell Island, Windy Bay, and a National Parks reserve in South Moresby.
Despite a declared six-week moratorium on logging permits on Lyell Island, logging continues right down into the area sought for a national park. Last month the Hon. Member for Okanagan-Similkameen (Mr. King) had a letter published in British Columbia which falsely claimed that the B.C. Tory caucus was "unanimous in its support of the western forest products solution". That Tory Member forgets that at least
April 3, 1987

five Tory MPs do not hold that view, including yourself, Mr. Speaker.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) met with the B.C. Premier recently and obtained his support for an early settlement of the boundaries for the park reserve, including all of Lyell. Next week the federal and provincial Ministers of the Environment meet to finalize the boundaries and move forward with compensation and economic development projects for the park, Sandspit, and the islands generally.
However, just hours before a settlement we discover that there are secret plans to go ahead and log Windy Bay, other parts of Lyell Island, and the small islands to the north and west of Lyell. Canadians were led to believe that all of Lyell would be included. We are sadly learning otherwise.
Mir. Speaker: I must say that all Hon. Members know that the matter raised by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) is of course a very serious one about which many people have very strong views.
However, I would ask Hon. Members when they make statements not to refer in one way or another to what they may think the view of the Speaker may be on any particular matter. I would ask for that courtesy.

subsubtopic: A DEFENCE OF TRADITIONAL CANADIAN FAMILY-STATISTICS QUESTIONED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today in defence of the traditional Canadian family, the family which many Members opposite have said is like the dinosaur- extinct. I refer, of course, to the recent statements pertaining to the issue of child care, statements that only 16 per cent of families are traditional, by which it is taken to mean that only one parent goes to work and the other parent stays at home to care for the children.
I do not know from where Hon. Members have obtained their information. However, I would point out that the figure obviously does not relate to families with young children. In fact 44 per cent of families with children under the age of three years have one spouse at home full-time. Thirty-eight per cent of families with children three years to five years of age have a spouse at home full-time.
The traditional Canadian family is not dead. I should like to know who the Opposition is including in its figures. Is it including retired couples, or Aunt Mabel in the nursing home?
In so far as these figures relate to families with young children, they are way off base.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF CANADIAN SPACE AGENCY-POSITION OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a Member of Parliament from the Montreal area, I would like to join and support the Montreal Economic Community, municipal authorities in Montreal, the Leader of the Parti Quebecois Mr. Pierre-Marc Johnson, and Quebec's Premier Mr. Robert Bourassa in saying unequivocally to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) that we do not and never will accept the argument being developed by the Conservative Government to justify their refusal to locate in Montreal the space agency, for the reason that the Government of Canada just helped save jobs at the GM plant in Sainte-Therese.
Mr. Speaker, it is important to remember that the grant extended by the Quebec Government is helping save the 5,000 jobs in Montreal, while the Federal grant is aimed at helping save 2,800 jobs in Ontario and create 2,600 new jobs.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say to this Tory Government that the whole Quebec population will unanimously refuse to be conned once more by this Tory Government.

subsubtopic: CREDIT CARDS-HIGH INTEREST RATES CHARGED BY DEPARTMENT STORES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the past two weeks three chartered banks have heeded Parliament's call to cut interest rates on credit cards.
When are major retailers and department stores going to show that they have some responsible corporate citizenship too? They are still levying a whopping 28.8 per cent interest on unpaid balances whether a balance is $40, $400 or $4,000. One department store pushes its charge cards by saying it will help the consumer with a new home, a new baby, a new decor, a new hobby, a new style, but it does not add "at the same old interest rate". Another says that it is easier and faster to use the charge card than to write a cheque. It is, Mr. Speaker, until you pay 28.8 per cent interest.

CHANGES TO BRITISH COLUMBIA LABOUR LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Social Credit Government in British Columbia proposed radical changes to B.C.'s labour legislation. These proposals will bring sweeping changes to union certification, dispute settlement, the protection of workers by unions, and they will increase the Government's powers to intervene in labour-management disputes.
The changes were introduced with absolutely no consultation with the B.C. Federation of Labour which represents a quarter of a million workers in the province. They are ill considered, disruptive proposals that will create mistrust, insecurity, and increased conflict.
We in the New Democratic Party call on the B.C. Government to withdraw these drastic changes to labour law, to study far more carefully and thoroughly any future changes to labour legislation, and to consult fully with the B.C. Federation of Labour before making any changes in the province's labour legislation.

subsubtopic: CHILDREN IN KINDERGARTENS AND NURSERY SCHOOLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has been a lot of recent media comment on the dangers of the so-called informal market in so far as child care is concerned. I would like to point out that some of this unlicensed care includes nursery schools, junior kindergartens, and kindergartens, none of which are considered licensed.
Teachers in these facilities are often better educated than licensed child-care workers. May I ask you, Mr. Speaker, and the Canadian public, are we really to believe that children in these facilities are at risk?

program have a target date, percentages, and the specific purpose of implementing and supporting what we in Canada are doing to come to grips with this very important ecological issue?

CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY STATIONING OF TOXIC CHEMICAL FREIGHT CARS ON FLOOD THREATENED BRIDGE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is directed to the Minister of Transport. Will he launch a full public inquiry into the incredible action of CPR officials in placing 17 rail cars, including 13 filled with toxic chemicals, on the railway bridge at Perth-Andover in order to counterbalance the pressure from ice and flood water? Will the Minister be launching a full public inquiry to get to the bottom of this issue?

subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY STATIONING OF TOXIC CHEMICAL FREIGHT CARS ON FLOOD THREATENED BRIDGE

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA SPORTS FISHERY TAGGING PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the chinook or spring salmon stocks of Canada's West Coast are a very precious mainstay of our recreational fishing industry and are harvested as well by our commercial and native fishermen. speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: COMMEMORATION OF SEVENTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF THE BATTLE OF VIMY RIDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, next week we will be marking one of the most important dates in our history. Seventy years ago this Thursday, April 9, Canadians from coast to coast, standing shoulder to shoulder, moved forward against the strongly entrenched positions at Vimy Ridge in France. By the end of the day, the Canadian Corps stood triumphant at the top of the ridge.
This triumph is the acknowledged birth of Canada as a nation. Brigadier General Alex Ross was to describe what happened in this way:
The barren earth erupted humanity. From dugouts, shell holes and trenches
men sprang into action, fell into artillery formations, and advanced to the
ridge ... It was Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific ... I thought thenthat in those few minutes I witnessed the birth of a nation.
Our victory was not without cost. Over 10,000 Canadians were casualties in the one day battle, 3,500 of whom were killed. Four Canadians earned the Victoria Cross, three of them posthumously.
As part of my mandate to perpetuate the memory of Canada's wartime sacrifice, I will be leading a delegation of 10 Vimy veterans to Vimy Ridge next week. We will be paying homage to those who fell at Vimy, and, indeed, to the over
66,000	Canadians who were killed during the Great War.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I wish to make all Hon. Members aware of a very special carving now on display in the lobby outside the Chamber. This carving, a replica of the Canadian Memorial at Vimy, was presented to me by the Royal 22nd Regiment. It was expertly crafted by Master Warrant Officer J.A.P.R. Laplante of the 22nd's 1st Battalion. I am told that Master Warrant Officer Laplante put in well over 1,000 hours of carving time. The result is simply magnificent. I therefore recommend it to Hon. Members' attention very much indeed.

subsubtopic: COMMEMORATION OF SEVENTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF THE BATTLE OF VIMY RIDGE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: COMMEMORATION OF SEVENTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF THE BATTLE OF VIMY RIDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the official Opposition critique for Veterans Affairs, I consider it a great honour and take great satisfaction in joining the responsible Minister in commemorating that historic feat, seventy years ago on April 9, at the Battle of Vimy Ridge during the First World War.
Mr. Speaker, on that day, at 5.30 a.m. at sunrise, under a ceaseless barrage of fire, iron and steel, Canadian divisions
launched the attack on Vimy Ridge, headed by ten battalions marching abreast which lead the attack, while flurries of wet snow swept the cold and somber battle ground. April 9, 1917 was truly a landmark in our history as a nation.
Canada entered the First World War as a nation that was still young. It had always existed in the shadow and under the trusteeship of the two mother countries, France and Great Britain. However, when the Armistice was signed at the end of this terrible conflict, Canada had succeeded in carving out a niche for itself among the nations of the world and was recognized and invited as an independent country to attend the peace negotiations.
Mr. Speaker, blood and iron forged a new nation on that day, an independent Canada, a Canada that was respected and that earned the privilege of ranking among the great nations of this world.
Mr. Speaker, all Canadians are grateful to the 600,000 men and women who answered the call of their country during the First World War.
Vimy Ridge is a symbol of their sacrifice and their courage. That is why every year, so many Canadians go back to Vimy to attend a service commemorating this great battle, in front of the splendid monument that stretches up to the sky, as though to carry up to heaven our prayers commemorating all who fought at Vimy.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may quote the Right Hon. Mackenzie King, the Prime Minister at the time, who said in the House on March 27, 1923, before the monument was built, and I quote:
The future will look on the battle grounds of the Great War as the altars of a
holocaust, and none will shine more brilliantly in our memory and our history
than Vimy.
And that is also why the seventieth anniversary of the Battle of Vimy Ridge is a day of special celebration, a day of gratitude and a day of prayer.
Mr. Speaker, I want to wish the Minister "bon voyage", and 1 would ask him to express to the handful of men and women who will accompany him, as veterans who fought on April 9, 1917 at Vimy, our profound gratitude and our sincere thanks for the example they have set to the whole world through their acts of heroism and their exceptional courage.
We will be with you in our prayers.

subsubtopic: COMMEMORATION OF SEVENTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF THE BATTLE OF VIMY RIDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party, it is an honour to join the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees) and the veterans affairs critic of the Official Opposition in saying a few words about Vimy Ridge. If ever a conflict deserved to be called the war to end all wars, it was the 1914 to 1918 war. It was sheer slaughter from beginning to end. Canada alone lost over 60,000 troops in that war. We just have to look at Vimy Ridge itself to
April 3, 1987

appreciate the massive losses. It is estimated that 150,000 French troops were killed attempting to take it. Subsequently the British army also attempted to do so and was decimated. Then along came the Canadian troops to see what they could do against this seemingly entrenched natural fortress. It was quite a challenge for an inexperienced volunteer army. However, it was there at Vimy where all the divisions of the Canadian corps came together for the first time to fight as a single unit. The rest, as we say these days, is history. It is certainly history worth recalling and applauding.
There are over 14,000 veterans of the First World War here in Canada today. Next Thursday let us remember just what this very special group of veterans achieved for Canada. We should never forget their contributions and sacrifices and we should always be grateful.
At this point, Madam Speaker, I would like to offer my own congratulations to the Minister for heading that delegation of war veterans back to Vimy Ridge.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it has been a long time since the Budget and, apart from the fact that the Budget lends itself to being forgotten, many people may have forgotten what was in it. What was not in the Budget was brought home very dramatically to me yesterday when a Budget was brought down in the Newfoundland House. It is very timely for me to

April 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Rompkey
be able to make some comments on the federal Budget today because that Budget painted not only an austere picture but even a tragic picture of what is happening in this country.
I would like to read from an article in this morning's Globe and Mail which summarizes for Canadians what is happening in Newfoundland. Bear in mind that the Government in that province is of the same political stripe as the Government here in Ottawa. The article reads as follows:
Finance Minister John Collins presented a $2.8-billion budget yesterday that freezes construction of new government buildings and predicts dire consequences for Newfoundland's ailing economy unless Ottawa comes through with more money.
"The 1980s decade has not been kind to Newfoundland and Labrador." he said. "We should not be asked, nor would we agree, that our people should be thankful to receive half the Canadian loaf.
"After 38 years, we remain the archetypal have-not province."
I suggest that it is relevant that we are continuing the Budget debate today. I say in all sincerity to Elon. Members opposite that there is a responsibility for us here in this Chamber and on the treasury benches to be cognizant that there is a province in Canada that is in very, very serious financial straits. Some people would even say the province was on the verge of bankruptcy. I suggest that the treasury benches take a very close look at what is happening and at their own fiscal and financial policies.
Let me give some indicators of what is happening at the federal level. The Government told us in the budget debate and thereafter that something like 400,000 or 500,000 new jobs have been created. I remind the House that the Newfoundland unemployment rate is more than 20 per cent. With the exception of about 6 per cent, all of those new jobs have been created in central Canada. That is a very distinct reality. Given that one measure of the success of the Government's financial policies is job creation, then it has failed miserably.
The Government has not had a regional development policy. I have seen no evidence in this Chamber of any policy over the last two years. Between 1984 and 1986 the Government reduced regional development expenditures by 25 per cent. Not only that, there has been a consistent and conscious effort to cut government programs and spending. There may be a rationale for that, but I submit, as I have before, that when you have a national policy which cuts across the board without regard for its effect on the regions, then it is a double burden on those less favoured regions which depend more heavily on government services and programs. No one likes dependency but it is a fact of life. When you slash across the board you hurt the weakest. That is the reality. You cannot have a single policy. If you do, you entrench regional disparity. I again use the example of Procruste's bed. He was a Greek innkeeper who had one bed. If the guest was too long for the bed he cut the person to fit. If he was too short, he stretched him to fit. That is the policy of the Government for the whole country. I submit that when that happens you entrench regional disparity. That is exactly what is happening. That is why in my province,
which is not economically self-supporting, we now have a three-year freeze on construction, expansion and renovation of public buildings. The worst part of that is that it applies to nursing homes, hospitals and schools.
Two days ago my province celebrated 37 years in Confederation. When Joey Smallwood led the fight for Confederation in Newfoundland he told us we would gain the advantage of receiving services equal to the rest of the nation. Yet yesterday's budget in Newfoundland told us that for three years there is going to be a complete and absolute freeze on most new construction, including nursing homes, hospitals and schools. What is Confederation all about? Are we all equal? Do we have the right to expect services and policies from the Government of Canada which will advance our interests and allow us to develop as a people? That is not happening because the Government has absolutely no policy for regional development.
Let me give a few other examples. We have seen a cut-back in equalization payments. Those payments are a fundamental lever of federal policy for righting regional disparity across this country. Oh, yes, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) told us recently that something like $180 million in equalization overpayments, caused by demographic changes, will be forgiven. However, it is not new money. It is of no help to an ailing economy. There has been a cut in Established Programs Financing for education and health care. Newfoundland, as did the rest of the country, expected an increase of 7 per cent. That was the five-year agreement between the federal Government and the provinces. The federal Government unilaterally abrogated that agreement and instead of a 7 per cent increase we will receive only 5 per cent. That may seem trivial when you look at it superficially, but in Newfoundland it means we will receive $187 million less than we had expected or budgeted for schools and health services.
In delivering his budget yesterday the Newfoundland Minister of Finance said:
We should not be asked, nor would we agree, that our people should be
thankful to receive half the Canadian loaf.
1 repeat, the brutal reality is that for three years the expansion of nursing homes, hospitals and schools will be completely frozen. That is the tragic reality.
Newfoundland has the highest rate of taxes in Canada, including a 12 per cent sales tax, yet taxes will increase by $600 to $800 for the average family as a result of the last federal Budget. There has been a one-cent increase in the federal tax on diesel and aviation fuel.
The simple fact is that the Government has one single underlining principle, and that is to let the private sector do the job. Yet that is not working and it is time the Government woke up to that fact. We have a province which is struggling, not to progress but simply to stay alive. I cannot make that point too strongly. That is not rhetoric. 1 hope the treasury benches will realize that.
April 3, 1987

What initiatives has the Government taken? It has said that it believes oil will be the salvation of Newfoundland. I hope so, but there" is no evidence of that so far. Yes, it is true the Atlantic Accord was signed. Yes, it is true that $66 million has been spent on development as a result of that Accord. What we have not seen is any movement toward development of the oil field itself. We are told there is a deal in the making. We are told there is an offer. We do not know and that is part of the problem. We cannot get information on what the Government is doing and the hard cold facts of what it plans for the province. We are told there is a deal between Mobil and the federal Government. We are told that that deal will involve Mobil spending something like $900 million in a $4.3 billion development program for the Hibernia field. However, Mobil will be able to recover that investment after three years. That has been described as a jammy deal for Mobil. We do not know what that company's response will be. As far as we can tell, the Newfoundland Government has approved the offer. As far as we can tell, Mobil is studying the offer and will respond some time before June. Yet how many Newfoundlanders know the facts of that deal before it is announced, if it ever is? That is very important to us because our future will hang on it. What will the advantage of that deal be to the people of Newfoundland? As far as I can tell that is what the Government is hanging its hat on. We will have to be very vigilant over the next few months and ensure that we ask the proper questions and scrutinize this deal very closely indeed. There has been no consultation on this matter. It has been very difficult indeed to get information on what the Government is doing.
The Government has encouraged and possibly twisted the arm of Petro-Canada to go ahead with some drilling this year. We know that the SEDCO 710 will be drilling off the coast of Newfoundland this year. However, that rig would have to be out there anyway because, as I understand it, it is still under contract to Petro-Canada and it would have to be used somewhere, albeit not necessarily on the Grand Banks. Therefore, that initiative alone is no indication that there is a willingness and dedication by the Government to go ahead.
In the meantime the Government is going ahead with the privatization of the very arm of government which it is using to suggest that it is serious about the development of the oil field off Newfoundland. At the same time as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) announces the initiative by Petro-Canada to drill further on the Grand Banks, the Government is putting Petro-Canada up for privatization. I believe that is another indication of the ingrained philosophy which is not in the best interest of that province.
I believe the strength of Canada has been that we have always had a mixture of private and public sector initiatives, a mixed economy. Petro-Canada was created to take risks which other private companies would not take, to go where other private companies would not go, to take initiatives on behalf of
The Budget-Mr. Rompkey
Canadians. The very vehicle which was created for those purposes is now up for sale.
1 suggest that it is time the mentality of the Government change and it realize that the approach of solving regional disparity through the private sector is not working. The Government must come up with a different approach. It must reassess its position and ensure that it has policies which will help a province, not only to advance, but to hold the place it now has.
I have heard the Minister of Transport, who is Newfoundland's representative in the Cabinet, talk about the benefits of free trade. That is another initiative which the Prime Minister has said will be the salvation of the region. Yet there is no hard information as to how that free trade deal with the U.S. will impact on the regions. There are all sorts of indications that it will not be a help to the regions. The fact is that we are getting no clear indication from the Government on exactly what the facts are and what the impact will be.
I appreciate this opportunity to put those things on the record today because, in light of the Budget which came down in the province yesterday, it is urgent that this House and, in particular, the treasury benches, realize that the ball is in their court. The power is in their hands to advance a policy for that province which will not only enable it to make progress but enable it to remain in Confederation.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

speechtext:
Questions,
comments. The Hon. Member for Louis-Hebert.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, with all due respect to my Opposition colleague the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey), I would like to make a few comments and ask him a question about his speech.
First, he stated a number of times in his remarks that this . Government, our Government, had no regional development policy. I am personally very much surprised to hear him say such a thing, in view of the fact especially that since we came to power we have given concrete examples-and have results to prove it-that we are committed to developing the various regions across Canada.
Let me refer to an example that happened recently. When this Government awarded the CF-18 maintenance contract in the Montreal area, we thereby insured the future of aeronautics research there, at that specific location.
Currently, as vice-chairperson of the Committee on Research, Science and Technology, I am very well informed of this Government's future policies on scientific research and technological development.
And I can state, Madam Speaker, that together with the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Cote), who is to announce very soon a long-term regional development policy, the Government is currently consulting with various

April 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Rompkey
departments in order to put forward to Canadians a policy that will be of benefit, a policy that will not be a duplication, and that also calls for most departments to make suggestions to avoid duplication and to ensure that all regions and all department components come up with a development that will enable us to ensure the future of all Canadians, long-term wise and for years to come, into the 2,000's.
Madam Speaker, I would like to point out to the Hon. Member that he stated we have created almost no new jobs. 1 would like to tell him again that we have created at least
705.000	jobs, 80 percent of which are permanent.
Madam Speaker, he said that currently the economy is ailing. Well, if we have an ailing economy, this is quite a performance because under the Liberals the economy was dying.
Madam Speaker, I would like to ask a question to the Hon. Member for Grands Falls-White Bay-Labrador, as a Liberal Member. Instead of constantly suggesting that everything this Government is doing is wrong, I would be extremely pleased to hear at some point from him positive proposals to the Government for a better regional development policy.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You have been elected, Madam.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for her question and I do believe I have some very positive suggestions to make. With regard to new jobs, as 1 said in my remarks, it is true that new jobs have been created. The Government has said that it has created something like
400.000	new jobs in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Seven hundred thousand.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Seven hundred thousand new jobs, that is right, but I ask the Regional Minister how many jobs have been created in the Atlantic area. The fact is that statistics show that only 6 per cent of those new jobs have been created outside central Canada. That is exactly the point I am making. I am making the point that there is not a regional development policy.
If I had to make a specific suggestion it would be to restore the balance to the regional development envelope which was decreased by $3 billion between 1984 and 1986. If the Member does not want to take my word for that she can take the word of the Premier of Newfoundland who is a Member of the same Party as Hon. Members opposite. The policy of the Government is, first, to hope to hell that the private sector will do the job all across the country and, second, if you have to have a regional development policy of any kind, let it be broker politics. It is not possible to operate a country on brokerism. There must be a consistent, co-ordinated and well developed policy that recognizes that there are less favoured people and more favoured people in this country. That is the reality. If regional development simply operates on brokerism and the
Government simply operates its regional development policy on the basis of where it will get votes, it will not work. We do not have any votes and cannot offer the Government anything. We only have seven seats in Parliament so what power do we have in broker politics?
Our only hope is the vision that the creators of Canada had in 1867 and the vision of people like Joey Smallwood in 1949. That is our only hope that we will get a fair deal.
I made the point that we are not getting a fair deal because the jobs are not being created in Atlantic Canada. The problem lies in the fact that the regional development envelope of the Government has decreased.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was very interested in the remarks of the Hon. Member. I was reminded of the figures I have heard which show that the education tax in Newfoundland and the other Atlantic provinces is considerably higher as a proportion of the gross domestic product than in the other provinces. As well, personal income tax is considerably higher as a proportion of provincial revenue than it is for other provinces. This certainly underlines the point the Hon. Member has been making, that there is a very serious situation facing the Atlantic Provinces even in regard to equalization payments. I agree with his points, particularly in response to the question.
As someone from Toronto, I can say that it is not enough to acknowledge that there are a lot of jobs in Canada and ignore the fact that hardly any of them are in Newfoundland or the Atlantic Provinces.
There is another matter on which I would like him to comment. Vast resources have been taken and are still being taken from Newfoundland and Labrador. These include mineral, forest, hydro, fish and oil resources which at a glance may seem to make the people of that province at least well served, if not rich. I must come to the conclusion that those resources are not under the control, let alone ownership, of the people of Newfoundland and Labrador. Will the Member comment on the budgetary action, or tax action, or other action which might be taken, not merely to put revenue or income into Atlantic Canada's hands but to restore to them control of those resources which they used to control in their own provinces?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is an excellent question and I thank the Hon. Member for it. If I could put it simply, I would say that when one has very little to begin with one has to mortgage very heavily. We have had so little to invest that we have had to mortgage heavily throughout our history. That fact remains. For example, the investment in mineral development has been by large American firms. While there are some royalties and jobs from this, the levers of economic power are in the hands of large American multinationals.
April 3, 1987

It is a fact of life that we are linked inextricably with the Province of Quebec with respect to hydro power. We share the same continent and we share the Ungava Peninsula. If that power is to flow to a reasonable market, it must go through the Province of Quebec. Therefore, we had to mortgage again and, while one may agree or disagree with it, that mortgage is a fact of life.
What about the fish resource? While I may sound partisan, as a result of initiatives this Party took when we were the Government of Canada, Newfoundland is finally regaining some financial control in the fishery because in the past two weeks Fishery Products International-a company we set up as a majority partner when we were the Government-has been privatized and is very profitable. That is what must happen. The levers of financial power, whether private or public, must go back to the people and that process must be accelerated in all those resources.
The point I have been making to the Government is that a laissez-faire approach will not necessarily work all across the country. There are areas which need the economic power of the Government in order to make progress. I believe that is still true in my area, as it has been not only for decades but for centuries.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
On February 18, 1987, Madam Speaker, our Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) tabled his Budget, his message to the Canadian people. He was contemplating expenditures of some $122 billion. The Minister indicated on that occasion the additional taxes which he would impose on Canadians and, for the first time, we witnessed a budgetary tax increase of less than 1.5 per cent of total spending, that is to say, less than $1.5 billion out of $122 billion in total spending, which proves that our Government is well aware of the need to ease as much as possible our taxpayers' burden. Also, Madam Speaker, 1 should add that out of this $1.5 billion, we are going to obtain $1.2 billion from major corporations; those paying over $15,000 per month in
The Budget-Mr. Fontaine
deductions at source from their employees paychecks, will have to pay these deductions twice a month, so that the Government will collect $1.2 billion more without Canadians having to pay a single cent out of their own pockets.
Finally, the Government will also increase the prices of gas and tobacco, for a total of approximately $1.5 billion out of $122 billion.
Before breaking down further these revenues and commenting on the Budget, it is advisable to consider what we are going to do with this $122 billion budget.
There are three major spending categories, and the most important one, the one to which our Conservative Government will allocate the greatest funds, concerns social programs. As a matter of fact, Madam Speaker, out of a $122 billion budget, $57 billion will go to the needy through all sorts of social assistance and benefits, including old age security pension, unemployment insurance, youth assistance, etc.
We are going also to spend $28 billion to pay the interest on the debt which was accumulated by our predecessors, leaving $37.1 billion to meet the needs of the other Departments.
With its message, our Government has shown Canadians its great concern for gradually reducing the Government's deficit. In 1985-86, our deficit was $34.4 billion; it was $32 billion in 1986-87, and we foresee for 1987-88 a deficit of $29.3 billion.
Madam Speaker, it should be emphasized that we have managed to reduce our deficit and as much as 63 per cent of that reduction resulted from cutting down on Government spending through better quality management. This was formally acknowledged by Mr. Dye, the Auditor General of Canada, when he tabled his first report. Everybody knows that, every time the Auditor General tabled his reports dealing with quality control and Government management, he used to criticize the previous Government and the Liberals for their mismanagement. Now in our case, Madam Speaker, for the first budget which we were entirely responsible for in this House, the Auditor General has indicated that we have considerably increased the quality of our financial management.
Our budget has taken into account, Madam Speaker, a very small increase of program expenditures, that is we have increased the program expenditures by less than 2.8 per cent, or at a lower rate than the inflation rate which is between 3.9 and 4.1 per cent. That again represents a very significant effort.
And what are the tangible effects of that control and reduced deficit?
Firstly, we have contributed, and every Canadian can appreciate it, to a very significant reduction of interest rates. As we know, Canadians will never forget that in 1981, they paid 22 to 24 per cent interest rates on their loans and we have seen last week that the bank rate had decreased to 7 per cent.

April 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Fontaine
So if we compare the interests paid under the Liberal Government and those paid today, there is a very significant difference. All Canadians can appreciate it when they borrow to purchase durable goods such as a car, a house, etc. And this has surely and clearly an effect at the beginning of each month when Canadians make their mortgage payments.
There are also other tangible consequences of our good management. 1 now refer to the 705,000 new jobs created by Canadians and not by the Government. The Government has offered favourable conditions to Canadian entrepreneurs and businessmen, encouraging them to invest in this country. This has an entirely different effect than that of the infamous Canada Work programs under which the Liberal Government created jobs lasting four months and then the people would be back on become unemployment for eight months. As opposed to that, we got organized, and our message was heard, especially by small businesses because 70 percent of those
705.000	new jobs that were created are due to small and medium size businesses. And that, Madam Speaker, we achieved despite the slump in the international price of oil. That oil price slump created many problems in Western Canada, and despite a very significant level of job losses in the oil industry and oil and gas exploration, we still created
705.000	jobs. And that job creation was also achieved despite the very sharp decline in the prices of farm commodities. That has created many problems for our farmers, but despite all that we succeeded in creating many new jobs. And those
705.000	new jobs were also created despite an increasingly protectionnist mood in the United States against some of our exports.
All of that, Madam Speaker, clearly was favourably reflected in terms of the level of economic recovery in Canada. And we are going to pursue along that road, we will pursue deregulation, and we also will pursue privatization of some corporations. Let us remember how much de Havilland and Canadair have cost Canadians. Billions of dollars were sunk, and the Liberals even passed special legislation to write off Canadair liabilities billions of dollars that were later transferred to the Canadian Government deficit.
We are going to keep on improving legislation, and we are not going to put forward legislation that solely reflects the interests of marginal people in this country. Our legislation, our positions will increasingly be aimed at the total Canadian population, because the total Canadian population pay the bill when we legislate in some areas. So we will take that total population into account.
We will keep on modernizing our financial services. We made possible, actually we brought barriers down, we opened the doors between the various financial institutions like brokerage firms, insurance companies, banks, so that you will now be able to obtain various financial services from a single business place. This is simply in tune with the new, modern ways of doing business, a kind of attuning Liberals did not feel
to be pertinent. We have done it. And we did it while protecting for instance services offered by our insurance agents, our local insurance brokers who are still exclusive insurance retailers.
In addition to our goals of good management and deficit control, we will remain committed to two major national matters. I am referring to the matter of trade liberalization with the United States. I will also refer to the matter of tax reform. It is important for our Government to sign an agreement with the United States to ensure that our exporters, who over the past few years have developed a market worth $95 billion a year ... It is important for us to keep this market and, with the Government's help, we are going to keep it through a definite agreement with our American neighbours, in spite of the negative attitude of both the Socialists and the Liberals.
Moreover, Madam Speaker, we are going to make a sustained effort to come up with a tax reform in an attempt to discourage some of them who seem partial to the American tax system from leaving Canada permanently to pursue their business in the United States which would be detrimental to our country. Therefore, we are going to make sure that our tax legislation will fit within the North America framework to prevent this brain drain. Through our tax proposals, we are going to encourage the ant rather than the cicada. You certainly know the fable, Madam Speaker. The cicada sings all summer long but comes winter and it is totally without resources. It decides to turn to its neighbour, the ant, which is more the thrifty type. So far, our tax system favoured for decades by the Liberals did not encourage the ant but the cicada. It did not encourage Canadians to invest, to use their savings to create new business ventures, because they had to pay too much tax on their savings. We, on the other hand, understand that the ant is more important than the cicada; consequently, we intend to give back to the ant the desire to get involved in business. We are going to amend our tax system accordingly.
Madam Speaker, we are also going to ensure, through our tax proposals, that Canadians pay significantly less income tax.
The Minister of Finance's message is directed also to Quebecers. We can say that Quebecers will enjoy an international banking centre, and those in Montreal East will witness the rebirth of the petrochemical industry. We know that the F-18 will be built in Montreal and that shipyards in Eastern Canada and Quebec will get a new start. There have been formal commitments of over $1 billion to Versatile Vickers shipyards, in Sorel, and my own shipyards in Levis and Lauzon.
The day before yesterday, Madam Speaker, this Government also announced that the plant in Sainte-Therese-and I see that my colleague, the Minister for External Relations (Mrs. Landry) is here-would continue to employ 5,500 Quebecers in Quebec and that the same plant would also guarantee 5,400 jobs in Ontario. Many of these jobs are in the riding of the Leader of the NDP, the Hon. Member for
April 3, 1987

Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), who did not make the slightest gesture to co-operate with our Government on reaching an agreement with the union so that the Government of Quebec and our Government could each contribute SI 10 million. The Leader of the NDP did nothing at all, nor did he intervene when we made our proposals on the pharmaceutical industry.
And what about the position taken by the members who are supposed to comment on our budget? 1 am thinking of the Elon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) who had nothing to say about the international banking centre. Madam Speaker, he knows what I am talking about. 1 am referring to an article that appeared in Le Devoir on January 30, 1987: "The banking centre project is unacceptable". That was the Elon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides. And that from a Quebec Member and a former Minister of Finance in the Quebec Government! The Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides did not take a very clear position either on the F-18 issue. And the same applies to his remarks on our trade with the United States. He ignores the position taken by his colleagues in the Quebec Government who are of the same political persuasion. He is at odds with the position taken by the President of the Liberal Party of Canada, Mr. Roberts, and we would have appreciated a more clear-cut position on his part in the matter of the Sainte-Therese plant.
Maybe that is why the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides has to force people to come and listen when he is a guest speaker. I would like to quote part of a letter that was sent to people in the riding of Saint-Jean by the Liberal Party of Canada. There was a complaint about the absence of elected officials and mayors. The letter goes on to say: "Considering that situation-the fact that they stayed away for two years- your presence or absence on May 1, 1987 at our supper will be noticed and noticeable". Elected officials are being forced to come and finance the Liberal Party, probably with the proceeds of municipal taxes.
And what about the party leader's comments on our Budget? He has no comments at all except for a few negative remarks. I think that before trying to comment sensibly on our Budget, he should first control his caucus. He should show he takes a clear stand on our negotiations with the Americans, on Canada's defence and on tax reform, which is a way of keeping capital and human resources here in Canada for the benefit of Canadians.
The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) may laugh at this, but I would like to listen to his response later today. When the Leader of the Liberal Party talks about the Budget he should tell us just how he would pay the $11.3 billion his day care program would cost. And how would he pay for his regional development distribution program? That I would like to know. I would also like to hear what he has to say about former Canadian Government Finance Minister Macdonald teaming up with Mr. Lougheed of Alberta to
The Budget-Mr. Fontaine
support the firm position of Canadian businessmen in favour of free trade.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Resign, incompetent!

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We do not hear the Leader of the Liberal Party talk about that. How much are we going to have to pay for the guaranteed income scheme they proposed in caucus? We do not hear him talk about that.
He should talk about the finances of the Liberal Party of Canada before commenting on anything else. In conclusion, Madam Speaker, if I may I should like to say a few words about the socialists, for I have something for them as well even though few of them are in the House today. They ought to shed some light on their own sources of financing. Let them tell us why they continue to remain silent about the fact that they obtain their funds in a way which is probably questionable, illegal, from Canadian workers' pay deductions. Madam Speaker, I would refer to the July 1986 ruling of Ontario Supreme Court Justice Wise that it was against the law to draw funds from the union dues of Canadian workers who do not belong to a union.
I would like to hear their side of the story. I would also like them to comment on their new awareness, their new understanding of the Province of Quebec. In 1981 they ignored Quebec, they did not know our province is different, but now they are prostituting themselves in a way, Madam Speaker, by telling us that Quebec is not a province like the others.
My last words are about their convention where they had 43 delegates from Quebec, a province with 75 ridings. They did bring a lot of western Canadians east to Montreal, but for their own convention they were unable to attract as many delegates as there are ridings. So before they lecture us, Madam Speaker, I would like to hear their explanations about the fact that they represent Quebec as well.
What is their position on Labrador, Madam Speaker, on aircraft test flights? I see that my time is up. I conclude by sending a message to the Party leader: Let him explain how come a socialist can draw a salary of $101,700, be driven around by a chauffeur, and still remain a socialist? That is food for thought.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question to put to my colleague. At the outset of his comments, he congratulated the Government for having collected $1.2 billion, thanks to its famous conjuring trick of which everyone is aware today since even financial experts are criticizing the Government for having manipulated the financial data in the budget.
Considering that my colleague has praised the Government, I am compelled to put to him the following question: Of course, everyone agrees that the Government is levying $1.2 billion from businesses. I should like also to point out to him that a building contractor in Quebec with 20 employees is also subject to that new measure which does not increase taxes nor reduce expenditures. However, during the financial year, the Government will be collecting $1.2 billion before March 31,

April 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Fontaine
1988 and what will be the effect of such a measure in the next budget between April 1, 1988 and March 31, 1989 after being levied only once? Is it not a red herring? The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) had to collect $1.2 billion to reduce or at least give the impression of reducing his deficit under $30 billion, but what is the purpose of such manipulation which is not approved by accountants themselves?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not understand why the expert in small and medium size businesses of the Liberal Party, the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano) cannot explain and understand how the Government without increasing taxes will collect $1.2 billion.
As you know, Madam Speaker, business people try more and more to accelerate the turnover of funds and to speed up the collection of accounts receivable. What is true for private enterprise is also true now for the Canadian Government. It is only sound management that Canadians be now asked for a timely and accelerated remittance of source deductions, because payroll deductions do not belong to businesses. From the moment the deductions take place, they belong to the employee, Madam Speaker, and all we proposed was to move to twice-monthly remittances, thus saving us some expenses and increasing our cash, our revenues by $1.2 billion.
Finally, I have this to say to the Hon. Member who just accused our Government of fiddling the accounts. I have already explained that there was no such thing, but I would like to remind him about the playing around of the Liberals when they wanted to conceal losses to the tune of billions of dollars that Canadair and de Havilland had accumulated. They passed a legislation that waived those losses which they included in Canada's consolidated deficit. That's tampering with the accounts. As well, I would like to refer my Liberal colleague to previous Auditor General's reports. Year after year, he pointed out that important and significant expenses were not accounted for, objecting to the fact that the Government would defer until later years the inclusion of theses expenses, and noting that liabilities did not show some well identified debts. Then, Madam Speaker, one could talk about manipulation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest to what my colleague had to say. I am slightly worried that he should get so hot under the collar; this does not do his blood pressure any good, and as I manage to remain quite calm in this House, Madam Speaker, as you have surely noticed, you can understand my concern.
I would like to ask the Hon. Member opposite, on the same subject to which the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano) referred when he asked him a question earlier, a very important question, which is normally the case, as you well know, when the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou gets on his feet, I would like to ask him the following question regarding payroll deductions which are then remitted to the Federal Government and which are now to be paid twice a month rather than once. The Hon. Member will recall that the
Canadian Association of Municipalities had recently written a letter to the Minister of Finance, and had in fact met with the Minister some time before the Budget was tabled, at which time it had asked him to channel supplementary funding to municipalities to improve municipal infrastructures. What happened in fact, Madam Speaker, as you well know, given your objective and non-partisan stance, and as the Hon. Member opposite knows also, I am sure, what happened was that the Government brought in a Budget which took more money away from already impoverished municipalities which needed extra funding and had informed the Federal Government of their needs only a short time before. Can the Hon. Member explain why his Government has taken money away from municipalities rather than give them the money they had asked for?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Firstly, Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) would be well advised to get acquainted with the Canadian Constitution and understand it, because it does not provide for development between municipalities and the Governement of Canada. Such a matter is a provincial reponsibility. I know that the Liberal party to which my colleague belongs has limited knowledge of the Constitution. Indeed, it entirely forgot the existence of a Canadian province in 1981. The Liberals should have known better.
In conclusion, I will say that the $1.2 billion that the Government is collecting, Madam Speaker, is money which is being collected more rapidly to which it is entitled and which was kept by the companies that were making to the Government monthly remittances of less than $15,000 in salary deductions. They will now make their remittances twice monthly. Now this is a measure of fine management and I am quite proud of it in spite of the allegations made by my Liberal colleagues.

speechtext: Order, please. The period for questions and comments has now expired. Debate. The Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to take part in this Budget debate. The Tory Budget before us is a two-Canada Budget. It divides Canadians into two groups, the rich and the rest of us. As some of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party have already pointed out, this Budget does little or nothing to address the inequities between the different regions in Canada, the subject of a speech made by the Hon. Member from Labrador this morning. It does little or nothing to end the terrible cycle of unemployment and poverty that grips Atlantic Canada, British Columbia, parts of the Prairies, northern Ontario and parts of Quebec. That cycle of poverty and unemployment is not limited to the have-not regions of Canada but it is certainly more prevalent.
Even in Toronto, we see the trend between a two-Canada society, one Canada for the rich and one for the rest of us. It is nowhere more visible than in my riding of Spadina where the golden windows of a bank tower look over the houses and flats of working people and of the rooms of those who have no work.
There was no direct mention of poor people, or poverty in the Budget of the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), nor was there a mention of poor people or poverty in the Speech from the Throne. This Government clearly would like to pretend that poverty does not exist, or does not exist in Canada. I can tell you, Madam Speaker, that poverty does exist in Canada, even in Toronto, even in Spadina within sight of the bank tower with the golden windows. There used to be an old song about how the banks are made of marble. That has gone out of style. Now we have gold windowed bank towers in Toronto, so the song will have to be updated.
However, in our Toronto, the Toronto for the rest of us, not for the banks and the rich, 165 food banks are needed to serve more than 200,000 free meals every month to those who simply do not have enough money to feed themselves. In our Toronto, 21,000 of those who depend on the food banks for nourishment are children. Those food banks did four times as
The Budget-Mr. Heap
much business last year as the year before. We are heading the wrong way.
There are 70,000 families currently waiting for subsidized housing, waiting in overcrowded and substandard housing. In our Toronto people are living and sleeping in the streets, in alley-ways, in abandoned cars and, in the wintertime, perhaps over a grate that brings up some warm air from some heating duct in one of the buildings. Others sleep in boarded up buildings. Increasingly the people who are forced to do this include young people, children as young as 10 or 12 years.
It is true that the nominal unemployment rate is declining in Toronto. I suggest that the official unemployment rate is a poor indicator of poverty. It is even a poor indicator of unemployment. We cannot really kid ourselves that the unemployment rate officially at 5 per cent or 6 per cent covers the people who have given up looking for jobs because they are not there. We cannot kid ourselves that it covers the people who are working part-time because that is all they can get, when what they want, are willing to do and need is full-time work. The Social Planning Council of Metropolitan Toronto has estimated that the real unemployment rate is probably one-third larger than the nominal unemployment rate in Toronto and elsewhere. In our Toronto, the number of people on general welfare has gone up 48 per cent over the past four years. In January, there were more than 50,000 people in metro on welfare.
Furthermore, our Toronto is a city where most women work. In our Toronto most working women have children. There is a tremendous shortage of affordable day-care, something that was noticed lately by a parliamentary committee, and then quickly forgotten since it was decided that the matter could be dealt with in a very slight and superficial way. The working women of Toronto know that that is not going to work. It will not support life as it can and should be lived by the working people in this country.	.
One of the ironies to which I have referred about the life in Spadina is that besides many such working people at the bottom of the scale and others at the middle of the scale, Spadina also contains Bay Street. It is my honour and privilege to represent Bay Street, the bank towers, the insurance headquarters, the oil company headquarters and many other such interesting institutions.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did they vote for you?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Those are the symbols of the other Canada. My colleague asks if they voted for me. The people who work in those bank towers do not live anywhere close. They live farther away among the elite. They vote for the elite somewhere else. I will add though that during municipal elections when they could vote for me I was elected four times as alderman in the ward and was never defeated.
This is the symbol of the other Canada, the symbol of Canada for the rich, the Canada that is so ably represented by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), by the Minister of

April 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Heap
Finance and by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner). This Budget serves the interests of the other Canada and ignores the needs of our Toronto. It did not deliver the programs which the working people of Spadina need. This Budget represented the needs of Bay Street. As a result of the Budget, for every $100 earned by a corporation the corporation will be paying $1 less in taxes than it did the year before. On the other hand, the working people in Toronto will each pay $2 more than last year in direct and indirect taxes on every $100 earned.
This Budget continues the regressive and unfair taxation measures that have marked this Government. The Hon. Minister of Finance increased taxes on the people who live in Spadina by an average of 13 per cent in this Budget. Combined with the increases in previous Budgets, the total tax increase borne by ordinary people comes to more than 50 per cent in the last two and a half years. The average family living in the shadow of the Toronto-Dominion Tower is being hit with a tax bill that is $1,300 higher than it was when the Government took office.
What about the companies with head offices in these bank towers on Bay Street? Who speaks for those companies? Of course, the Minister of Finance speaks for them. He used to work there and he speaks for them very ably. In this Budget, as in previous Budgets, he has reduced the share of taxes paid by Bay Street as compared to the share of taxes paid by the people who live in the rest of Spadina or in most of the rest of Canada.
The Government hopes to raise about $35 billion in new tax revenues by 1990. It intends to take almost all of that money out of the pockets of ordinary Canadians. It estimates new corporate tax revenues as making up only 1 per cent of that amount. Only 1 per cent of it will come from the wealthiest corporations in Canada. Is that fair? It is not. Is it good for the economy? We have been told to tighten our belts for another five, 10 or 20 years and that some day we will eat again. We should remember that it was consumer spending, not corporate spending, that brought us out of the last recession. The corporations were salting all their money away or spending it in other parts of the world. It was consumer spending that brought us out of the recession, and cutting back on the power of consumers to spend is not good for the economy.
My colleagues in the New Democratic Party have made recommendation after recommendation for ways the Budget could have been both fairer and more effective. The Budget could have seen that Bay Street carries at least as much of the tax burden as the people living in the shadows of those head offices. My colleagues in the New Democratic Party have advocated the reduction of the scale and importance of corporate tax expenditures. "Corporate tax expenditures" is an interesting term and refers to the money the Government spends on reducing a corporation's tax. In Toronto, we call them loopholes, give-aways, and ripoffs.
I would like to deal with one particular aspect of corporate tax expenditures. Last year, as the House may recall, the Hon. Minister of Finance was forced to revise his deficit forecasts. In the revision, about $1.2 billion of his shortfall was in corporate tax collections. That is to say, in a Budget that planned to reduce the tax burden on corporations, as compared to ordinary Canadians, he over-estimated the taxes corporations would pay. Last year, he over-estimated that figure by $1.2 billion.
How does the Minister of Finance, a smart businessman, make a $1.2 billion mistake? Last year the Hon. Minister said that it was because of unexpectedly low corporate profits. Had the Minister been somewhat more precise he would have said-as he said in the papers attached to the Budget papers which were not read by everyone-that the $1.2 billion error in 1986 was due to the unexpected application of something called a loss carry-forward.
What is a loss carry-forward? When a corporation has a loss or deduction that it cannot use in a given year for the purpose of reducing its tax, it can carry it forward and apply it to reduce its taxes in the following year. Working people are not allowed to do that. We cannot carry forward our losses in order to apply them where they would be more beneficial to us, but corporations, of course, can and they plan on it. The loss carry-forward means that the higher corporate profits are protected from taxes for many years to come.
If the Minister were to correct this problem, he would automatically find himself with a larger corporate revenue base for his taxes. Hence, he would have the ability to make the tax system fairer and to address some of the needs of the people who live in the shadow of Bay Street, whether that be in Spadina, Come-By-Chance or the Northwest Territories. If the Minister does not close up this and similar loopholes, then his promises of fairer taxes will ring as hollow in 1988 as they did in 1984.
It is hard to imagine anything less fair to the majority of Canadians than the present tax system. Already the majority of Canadian corporations pay no taxes. Some of them do not pay taxes because they are taking losses in the current year, and no one takes issue with that. However, many companies that do not pay taxes are profitable and do record positive net incomes on their balances sheets. Our NDP study of the tax system indicated that as many as half of all companies not paying taxes were profitable.
Some of these loopholes and tax expenditures might be justified if they provided efficient ways to create jobs, but they do not. Let me explain why this is so. First, if the House were to vote an appropriation of moneys as a grant for some purpose, there would be an elaborate accounting system that would give us a great deal of information on how effective the program would be. The Minister and the Auditor General would present reports to the House and perhaps the committee of the House studying the matter would look at how effective the grant would be. We might disagree but we would have the facts on which to base a reasonable argument. With these tax
April 3, 1987

expenditures, all we have is estimates in advance. We have no report and we have no real way of knowing if a company that has taken advantage of an investment tax credit has in fact created new jobs or has just shuffled the old ones around and pocketed the difference. We have no way of keeping track.
Second, studies have been done on the link between corporate tax cuts and private-sector job creation. These studies show a very, very weak link between the two, if any at all. In 1985, a study done by the Department of Employment and Immigration showed that if personal incomes taxes were cut by $1 billion, five times as many jobs could be created than would be created if corporate income taxes were cut by the same amount. That study was done by this Government and it was ignored. The same study indicated that if government spending were to be increased by $1 billion, six times as many jobs would be created as would be created by cutting corporate taxes.
Did the Government do that? Of course not. Instead, it has effectively reduced the portion of the tax burden paid by corporations while increasing that which is paid by individuals. This continues the trend followed by the previous Government ever since 1950. In 1950, the amount of income tax contributed by individuals and the amount contributed by corporations was about equal. Now, the immensely wealthy corporations contribute only one-quarter of the amount that is contributed by individuals to income tax. The Government has pushed that process still farther in the wrong direction.
What do I advocate? What should the Government do? It has obviously missed many chances already. It has missed the chance to announce specific employment targets, milestones on the road toward a goal of full employment for all Canadians. It has missed the chance to announce programs aimed at providing quality day care where it is needed. In this Budget, it missed the opportunity to increase the stock of housing for the homeless. It has failed to address the needs of the homeless in Toronto and elsewhere.
The Hon. Minister of Finance has reserved for himself the right to correct some of the inequities in this Budget. We hope he will address the needs of the people who live in the shadow of Bay Street, whether their address is Spadina, Come-By-Chance, or the Northwest Territories. I call on the Minister to right some of the wrongs in the tax system as embodied in this Budget.
I particularly call on him to undertake the following steps. First, he should establish a detailed annual accounting of the cost and benefits of this type of tax expenditure so they can be evaluated on the same basis as other government expenditures.
Second, he should restore a fairer balance in the tax system between what individuals give and what is given by the corporations and then cancelled through tax giveaways. We should never again hear the horror stories of profitable corporations who escape all or most taxes year after year. We
The Budget-Mr. Heap
have that situation in Spadina. At least two banks in some years paid no tax, although they each made hundreds of millions of dollars in profit. The Government of the day had the gall to give them, by way of a law made for its friends, a tax credit.
Third, the Minister ought to consider a minimum income tax on profitable corporations. He knows that consumer spending has been the driving force in pulling us out of the recent recession. To continue raising taxes on ordinary Canadians threatens our ability to extend that recovery. It threatens to return us to the recession. Tax expenditures on large corporations, which do not have to account for how they spend that money, do not help.
I see you are indicating that my time is nearly finished, Madam Speaker. I want to briefly mention three more points which should be considered. First, with tax reform of the kind I have described we would increase disposable income and the needed consumer spending. Second, we would have more money to deal with the social programs cut back by the Government, as represented by the Save Our Summers demonstration yesterday noon. When we have done that we might find that we had a little money to start reducing the deficit. The important thing in all of this is to build toward one Canada. Instead of polarizing Canada between the rich and the rest, we could build a Canada with equity in opportunity and condition for the people in Spadina, in Come-By-Chance, the Northwest Territories, the Gaspe, indeed, in every part of Canada where there are poor people.
