speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it has been very worth while to listen to the remarks of my hon. friend, particularly because I had the pleasure of living in his riding for 10 years. It was a Liberal riding through most of that time, but I think it has gotten better recently. One thing characteristic of the Hon. Member is his concern for those who can be described as the poor. It is a concern that I am sure all of us share. Where we will disagree is in the way we attempt to meet the problem he has identified.
I think it is very important to recognize that this Canada of ours is not divisible by two. It is a misrepresentation of the Canadian scene for the NDP to say it is divided between the rich and poor. In between those extremes there are so many people of varying degrees of affluence and accomplishment that it is simply distorting beyond all recognition the Canadian scene to speak as he did. Where we have to get together is on how to cope with the problem suffered by a too large minority of our fellow Canadians. I suggest that, as correct as many of the points that he made were, there are some things which need to be added to the record. In the brief time allowed me I want to do that.
First is the way in which the economic policies of this Government have added to the prosperity and increased the number of Canadians who have raised themselves up out of

April 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Heap
poverty through gaining employment and being able to provide for their families. Through their spending they contribute to the prosperity of others. That number has increased. That should be recognized for what it is. The most effective way of meeting the problem of poverty is meeting the problem of unemployment.
The second point I want to make concerns the way in which our social scene has been made a much more humane and helping scene because of the various pension reforms and other program improvements that have been part of this Parliament under the leadership of the Government.
The Elon. Member spoke about the inequities of the present tax system. In doing so he surely heralds the advent of the tax reform we will see in this Parliament. I certainly hope he will dedicate his support to that reform which we will hopefully see in this Parliament within this calendar year. I trust that reform will remove many of the inequities he has identified. More importantly, it will provide us with a tax system which will contribute to an increase in Canadian productivity.
One of the worst parts of our present tax system is the way it discourages the advance of productivity. That, unintentionally and indirectly, but nonetheless effectively, contributes to the poverty problem about which he is so concerned. The best way to deal with poverty is by improving the economy in a way in which more Canadians can have an active share. I think the forthcoming tax reform will give us that opportunity and I certainly appreciate the support of the Hon. Member.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his kind comments. I am aware that he lived in Spadina for some years. I am also aware that he did not choose to run for Parliament in Spadina.

speechtext: Aren't you lucky?

speechtext:
He likes the riding he is in better than Spadina. That is his choice. Perhaps he feels safer there.
In speaking about the poor he shows that he does not want to hear the facts I mentioned about the increase in Spadina, and other parts of Toronto, in the number of people who are forced to go to food banks for the day's food, including 21,000 children in Metropolitan Toronto. He did not refer to the families who are still waiting for subsidized housing. He did not refer to the social planning council's estimate of as much as 10,000 homeless people in Toronto. He talks, as do others on his side, about this jobs created figure. I will tell him that if he runs in Spadina he will have to face up to the fact that, notwithstanding all his statistics, there is a great deal of hunger and poverty in Toronto, including Spadina. People will ask him to answer for that.
He talked about the Government's record. He even had the comical nerve to mention pension reform. The pension reform his Government tried to implement was to reduce old age pensions. It was the NDP, with some help from the Liberals, that led the revolt of the senior citizens which forced the Hon. Member's Government to back down on that issue. He talked about tax reform. We have heard that talk since the election campaign of 1984 from the Hon. Member's Party. We have heard it promised every month since 1984. We have now had four Budgets with no tax reform of any benefit to poor people. According to the practice of the Hon. Member's Party tax reform means soak the poor and subsidize the rich. He claims that by doing that they will increase productivity.
As a factory worker for 18 years and a trade unionist, the productivity of Canadian working people is nothing of which 1 have any cause to be ashamed. With the equipment given them by the investors the Canadian workers have as good a record of productivity as almost any country in the world. To accuse Canadian workers of being unproductive and to claim that the unemployment and poverty which has been visited on some of them is a punishment for lack of productivity is false. We need not a whip to make the workers more productive, but a more rational division of the product of their labour. If the Hon. Member's Party is going to do that in its tax reform I will, of course, welcome it. However, I will also be very much astonished because it will be a 180 degree reversal of what it has been doing for the past two and a half years.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the comrade for Spadina (Mr. Heap) refer to his tax philosophy. He speaks of tax fairness, tax justice as far as tax sources are concerned, etc.
1 would like to ask him whether he considers it fair and just that the Socialist Party collect funds from compulsory salary deductions from workers who are not union members, and whether it is fair and just that the Socialist Party continue to ignore the judgment rendered in July, 1986 by Mr. Justice Wise of the Ontario Supreme Court. I would also like to add that his colleague from Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) already admitted that funding source. Finally, I would like to ask him whether it is fair that his Leader, the Leader of the Socialist Party refused to take a salary cut? He is still receiving $101,700. For a socialist to have a chauffeur and a limousine, we do not find that fair, Madam Speaker, and we would like to have explanations.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very glad to answer the Hon. Member's questions within the time available. With regard to Party contributions, as a trade unionist and factory worker, in non-union factories at first, I was not so much concerned about the small amounts which unions gave to the New Democratic Party as I was about the very large amounts given by the banks, oil companies, et cetera. To the best of my
April 3, 1987

knowledge they did not get the permission of their shareholders to do that. They did not ask their shareholders whether they wanted to give $50,000 to the Conservative Party and to the Liberal Party so they would have a hold on whichever Party formed the Government. To the best of my knowledge that was done without any of the control which is exercised by the members of my union, the Canadian Paperworkers Union, and other unions in Canada which can remove officers with a year's notice if the officers are mis-spending money. Therefore,
I believe that the trade unionist money which goes into election campaigns is under much better democratic control by the people who earn the money than are the huge donations made by the banks, insurance companies, oil companies and so on.
With regard to the court decision, I am going to wait to hear what the Supreme Court says. I remember a court decision 20 years ago which was against a union. The Royal York fired its employees who were on legal strike and cancelled their pensions. A judge said that according to the Master and Servants Act of 1513 the company had the right to do that. 1 remember that some powerful businessmen were horrified at that decision. There were some very left-wing trade unionists, further left than I, who rejoiced at that decision because it would have destroyed with one blow the whole system of labour relations built up in this country. Therefore, I will wait to see if the Supreme Court makes a wiser decision than did Judge Wise.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to take part in the debate on the Budget. Since the Budget came down in February I have received feedback from my constituents and heard comments from across the country on it. I am very pleased with the positive response on this Budget which was consistent with the direction of the Government and offered the people of Canada some real opportunities.
I do not want to spend all of my time today reviewing the facts and figures of the Budget because I want to discuss particularly its implications for my home Province of British Columbia. However, I will just remind my colleagues of the outline of the Budget. The most important thing about it is that it shows that this Government has control of the financial management of the country as has no government for a long period. That is what voters asked us to do when they sent us to office in 1984, and that is what we are doing. We all know of the situation we inherited. Spending had got out of control. It is like taking a huge ocean liner and trying to turn it around in the middle of the ocean. It takes some time to do it, but we have turned it around and are now going in the right direction.
To cite a few statistics in support of that, when we came into office in 1984, there was a deficit of $38.3 billion. In the past years we have been able to bring that down by 24 per cent. The projected deficit in the 1987 Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is only $29.3 billion. We would like it to go down even more and I know we will accomplish that with the fiscal management which the Government has undertaken. The real costs of Government are declining for the first time since the
The Budget-Mrs. Collins
Korean War. There has been a decline in the program expenditures of the Government. It is in the decline of program expenditures that we have been able to make the most rapid gains, and that accounts for 69 per cent of the decline in the deficit. As a result of the tremendous efforts by my colleagues in the Cabinet it is projected that by 1990-91 there will be a reduction of 15,000 positions in the Public Service.
What have been the results of this sound program of fiscal management? Some people expressed the fear that by taking what some may regard as relatively harsh measures to get spending under control we might see some adverse impacts. However, the exact opposite has occurred. Since September, 1984, over 700,000 new jobs have been created, by far the majority being full-time jobs. That is what Canadians want and need. Of great importance, too, has been the decline in interest rates which affect all of us when we have to borrow money to buy a home, a car, or invest in a business. A mere four or five years ago interest rates were at 22 per cent and people were really frightened. They could not realistically take a risk in buying a home or investing in a business. Now that interest rates are below 10 per cent and long-term mortgage rates are below 10 per cent, there has been a tremendous turnaround and, for the first time, young Canadians can look forward to the opportunity of owning their own home. That is probably the dream of every Canadian and we want to make sure that it comes true.
Low interest rates have meant increased investment in business because people are willing to take risks. New investment has come to Canada. Even with low interest rates, Canada is still very attractive because of the stability of the economy and the good management of the Government. This was recently verified in the Kanao Report by the group of Japanese businessmen who visited Canada late last year. They went throughout British Columbia and the country to meet with government officials and business people. Their report stated that they had found a new Canada which had a new spirit of entrepreneurship and productivity. They found diversification in industry and a stable investment climate. In fact, they recommended to their peers that Canada is a good place to invest. We look forward to the results of that investment in the years to come.
Another indicator of growth is the forestry industry, an industry that is so important in my home province. The estimates for 1987 are that capital investment in Canada's forestry sector will rise by 23.5 per cent. That is a spectacular increase despite the cries of potential doom and gloom we heard from the opposition Parties when we unfortunately had to deal with the 15 per cent export charge recently. Despite that export charge, the forestry business is booming, particularly in pulp and paper. British Columbia alone will benefit from 64 per cent of this projected increase in investment. New investments in the province's forestry sector is expected to reach $144.8 million, which will mean many more jobs.

April 3, 1987
The Budget-Mrs. Collins
There are projects planned for British Columbia that will have a tremendous impact on B.C. communities. Those are some of the results of this Government's efforts.
We should recognize how the efforts of the Minister of Finance and his ability to get financial issues and management on track allow other cabinet colleagues to support him with their initiatives.
Tax reform that will come forward later this spring is another initiative in the Budget about which we have heard a great deal. I look forward to that proposal and look forward to discussing its details when it is brought forward. We know that the Minister of Finance has already stated in his Budget Speech that we will be dealing with changes in personal, corporate and federal sales tax and that the emphasis will be on reducing the personal tax rate, reducing tax preferences and broadening the tax base. This will probably mean that lower income Canadians in particular will pay less tax, a policy which is indeed consistent with the other initiatives the Government took in its 1986 Budget, such as the $50 sales tax credit and the $300 child tax credit. We are focusing these efforts particularly on that group of people in our society who are facing greater difficulty because we want to help them. Our Government cares about all Canadians.
What has been the impact of this Budget and the Government's measures on British Columbia in the last two years? How do we ensure that British Columbia develops the potential that 1 believe it has in its people and resources? First, because we sometimes tend to overlook them and consider the negative, let us consider some of the positive aspects of what has happened in British Columbia in the last couple of years. Since September, 1984, 61,000 jobs have been created in British Columbia which is twice as many jobs in the 29 months since the Government took office than in the four years of the previous Liberal Government. Jobs have been created at a monthly rate of 2,103.
The unemployment rate has fallen from 15.1 per cent at the time of the election in 1984 to 13.3 per cent now. That is still to high and I hope to have an opportunity to expand on our plans to reduce the unemployment rate. Total unemployment, however, has fallen by 21,000 in the past two and a half years and we must ensure that it continues to drop.
There are other economic factors that are important to consider. For example, retail sales have risen by 6.8 per cent in the past year, and 18.7 per cent in the last two and a half years.
Urban housing is an important indicator in the economy and housing starts in 1986 were at their highest level since 1981. Construction commenced on 18,841 units, which means that those families, many of whom would be first-time buyers, can have a home of their own.
In December, 1986, manufacturing shipments were up 8.6 per cent from the same period in 1985, which is a tremendous increase. They are up 13 per cent since September, 1984.
The number of bankruptcies in the first month of 1987 was down 14.4 per cent compared to the same period in 1986. New incorporations are an indicator of small business activity which is a very important sector of our economy. They were up 11 per cent in 1985, which means 1,529 new businesses were started in British Columbia. At the same time, inflation was held at 2.8 per cent in Vancouver.
There are a number of other factors, but one of particular interest is tourism. International tourism sky-rocketed in 1986 and was up 80.6 per cent. We know that much of that is due to the spectacular success of Expo 86. However, it also means that the millions of visitors who came to Vancouver and British Columbia, and were exposed to the tremendous attributes and attractions of that city and province, will want to come back. We welcome them and their friends and family because beautiful British Columbia is the place to visit on a vacation. I am sure you will agree, Madam Speaker.
There are a number of initiatives which the Budget itself did not address specifically but which are being addressed by Ministers as they review their portfolios. Since the Budget in February we have been particularly pleased in British Columbia and my constituency of Capilano by the announcement that the new Polar 8 ice-breaker will be built at Versatile Pacific in North Vancouver at an estimated cost of $320 million. That is a major boom for the shipbuilding industry on the West Coast and shows the Government's commitment to that industry. It will mean jobs for 1,000 people and a certain future for the men and women and their families who work in that industry. They know they will be able to stay in British Columbia where they can enjoy the opportunities to work in their particular field. A long-term four to five-year contract will provide the shipbuilding industry with an opportunity to restructure and pursue other contracts, as there are interesting opportunities developing in the cruise ship business and other areas of shipbuilding which I know British Columbia will seek as well as future government contracts.
There was an even more recent announcement by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) with respect to an estimated $350 million program in the energy field which will also help British Columbia. Up until now the focus has been on Alberta. Let us not forget that there is a significant energy business in British Columbia, in particular in northern British Columbia around Fort St. John. This will mean a significant increase in exploration activity with drill rigs moving back in and with men and women working in that field. It will be necessary for suppliers to support the industry. These communities will have a chance to participate in greater economic activity than has been the case over the last year.
Those are just two announcements which the Government has made which are of significant importance to the West. Let us not forget the major initiative undertaken by the Government in its signing of the Economic Regional Development Agreement about a year and a half ago. This agreement covers
April 3, 1987

an important area and will infuse over $300 million into the forestry sector to assist in reforestation and silviculture. It is an agreement jointly shared by the federal and provincial Governments. It will also have an impact for the province in terms of tourism, agriculture, science and technology and small business. We are already seeing an impact on many of the activities that are associated with the ERDA. I will mention a few of them in a moment.
When we consider the economic structure of British Columbia we recognize that, traditionally, it has been resource-based. Forestry has been the main industry, and for many years mining was rated second in terms of industrial capacity. Agriculture has been important, as has the oil and gas industry to some extent. We are all aware of international trends which have caused a great many difficulties for all of these industries, especially in terms of the pricing of commodities in the mining field, and other problems we face in the forestry industry. In British Columbia we recognize that what we have to do is to build on the strengths that we have in these resource industries and find new ways to add value to those basic resources and to use new technologies in order to become more productive. We must have adaptive technologies which will help us add value to those basic resources. Some of this has been going on over the past couple of years. An interesting example which comes to mind is with respect to the forest industry which has implemented the use of computerized equipment. At a computerized sawmill of MacMillan Bloedel a computer can be given the specifications of a log, and in conjunction with another system which feeds in the order requirements, the equipment can automatically cut the log to meet the specifications of a particular order, whether it be for Japan, Germany or some other country. This has meant a tremendous increase in productivity and being able to meet market demands in a dynamic way. It is this type of technology that is vitally important to British Columbia.
We are also looking to other products. We have an interesting example in Prince George where a recent investment was made in a chopstick factory. Just a couple of years ago who would have thought that we could make chopsticks in British Columbia to export to Japan? However, we have the wood which, up until now, has been mostly waste wood, wood that was not being used. Through imagination and innovation some people got involved in making this investment in Prince George. They have produced a whole new industry with a number of people working in it.
What we need to do in British Columbia is to find markets. British Columbia is particularly reliant on trade. We are far from the markets of eastern Canada and the costs of transportation are high. The geography of the province makes it expensive to transport products even within the province. Thus, traditionally, we have looked to the U.S. for our markets and more recently to the Pacific Rim. This is why the new trade arrangements with the U.S. are vitally important to British Columbia. Opportunities which would open up new markets in
The Budget-Mrs. Collins
the Pacific Rim are equally important. These are the areas in which we need innovation and support from Government.
I believe it is not necessary to throw masses of money at a particular problem but that it is sometimes the identification of the obstacles to growth which are important. In some cases these obstacles have been in the form of protectionist measures or other problems which we have encountered in the United States as a result of countervailing practices. In the Pacific Rim we have been faced with similar sorts of restrictions, some of which are now being opened up, particularly for the forest industry. We are required to look not only at the products but able to match our ability with the markets.
We have to do more than say that we have a product and we want to sell it to a particular country, such as Japan or China. We have to get out and find out what it is that the people of China or Japan want and how we can develop or adapt our existing products to their markets. This is where I know the department of trade has been making great efforts to bring together our manufacturers and innovators with potential markets in this field.
I understand my time is up, Madam Speaker. There are so many other ideas which my colleagues and I have for the development of the economy of British Columbia which I look forward to sharing with Hon. Members as the weeks and months progress.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in listening to the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins), our Dr. Pangloss, I could hardly recognize that we come from the same province. The Hon. Member talked about job creation. I would like the Hon. Member to comment on the fact that in February the unemployment rate in Vancouver was 14.3 per cent, the highest unemployment rate in any metropolitan centre in Canada. The Hon. Member also talked about tax reform. Could she comment on the fact that between 1984 and 1991 projected Tory tax increases will amount to $20 billion in sales tax, $15 billion in personal tax and $128 million in corporate tax? In other words, corporate tax increases account for less than 1 per cent of the increased tax load that the Tory Government has loaded on individual Canadians. Does the Hon. Member think that is fair?
Will the Hon. Member comment on rumours that there will not be any exemptions on the business transfer tax which could be introduced as part of tax reform? This means that the business transfer tax would be added on to such basic items as food, children's clothing, housing or whatever. Does the Hon. Member believe that that business transfer tax should have exemptions or not? I am interested to hear the Hon. Member's comments.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first, with respect to the proposed business transfer tax, I really do not want to speculate on it. I think it is inappropriate at this time to comment on it since we do not know what the form of it will be or on what products or services it will be levied. It is appropriate to wait

April 3, 1987
The Budget-Mrs. Collins
until the plans come forward. There will obviously be a review process to determine that at that time.
The Hon. Member mentioned the unemployment rate in Vancouver. This is certainly something which disturbs me very much, as I know it disturbs the Hon. Member and other of my colleagues, since I know the rate in Vancouver is higher than it is in the province as a whole, which is perhaps rather an unusual situation. While not underestimating the difficulties this causes, I remind my colleague that some of the figures which are now showing up are as a result of people who worked at Expo last year. I know that in my own riding this has occurred. These people worked for six months at Expo. After that they were eligible for unemployment insurance which they are now collecting. They now show up on the records as unemployed. Not all of these people would have worked before Expo. They worked only during that six month period.
There may be a bit of a glitch there, and we may see that fall off on its own. Nevertheless, the unemployment figures for British Columbia are of concern to all of us, and that is why we think it is important, as the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) has indicated, that we move forward with the program of western diversification. That is why I and my colleagues from the British Columbia caucus have been spending a great deal of time working on this, to identify what we feel are the appropriate measures and the appropriate directions for this Government to take. We have to determine how we can be most helpful. We do not want to waste money. We want to use our resources most effectively to encourage job creation and meaningful activity-and long range jobs, not short-term make-work jobs. I personally do not agree with make-work projects.
I am very pleased with the Canadian Jobs Strategy Program, and particularly as it has been applied in my own Province of British Columbia. As I am sure my colleague is aware, during 1985-86, the Province of British Columbia received just under $1.7 billion under CEIC programs, an amount well over its percentage share of all CEIC programs.
Under the Canadian Jobs Strategy Program, 1 have found of particular value the Job Entry-Re-entry Program. It is a program that is very important in terms of getting those who are now unemployed back into the job market, and particularly so for young people who have quit school before attaining any marketable skills. Having the benefit of a nine month period in the job entry program in which to develop skills has resulted in an 80 to 90 per cent success rate in job placements in some of the projects in my riding for those young people. Similarly, many women have benefited from the Re-entry Option Program, a program that has allowed them to develop the skills and confidence to re-enter the workforce.
It seems to me that if these programs were expanded and extended, many of these people could develop the skills
necessary for even more highly paid jobs, instead of having to start at the bottom.
With those kinds of initiatives, along with other initiatives which I believe this Government will be bringing forward, we will see changes for the better in the unemployment rate over the next two years.
I am sure that my colleague opposite has ideas on how we can reduce unemployment. We would welcome his ideas on what we could be doing to assist in alleviating unemployment on Vancouver Island, an economy which is based on tourism and forestry. There may be other directions in which the economy of Vancouver Island can go, one of which might be to focus on the new information technologies, the new knowledge-based industries. These industries have a tremendous application for British Columbia.
The president of one of the major technology companies in British Columbia was recently asked why he was headquartered in Vancouver; why it was that he was not headquartered where the big markets are in eastern Canada. And his response was: "Because my employees want to live in Vancouver. With this kind of company, given the new communications technologies, it doesn't matter where the business is physically located. We can be where we want to be".
It is that kind of industrial activity, supported by strong post-secondary educational opportunities, that I think will be vital for British Columbia.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the intervention of the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins). I know that she pays very close attention to polls. Indeed, it has been alleged that, in embarking on any course of action in this House, she is governed largely by polls.
I heard her indicate, at the very beginning of her speech, that the latest Budget has been well received in Canada.
Considering what my colleague said earlier about the Panglossian nature of her intervention and her love of polls, we might even regard her as being "pollyannish".
1 am driven to ask a question about her response to the facts, which the polls have ascertained, with respect to the reception accorded the Progressive Conservative Budget. I have here the results of a poll reported in, among other places, The Ottawa Citizen of March 26, 1987. The headline is: "Most Canadians found latest budget forgettable". It wasn't well received, by any means. The opening paragraph of the article reads:
The federal government's latest "breathing space" budget in fact seems to
have left more Canadians yawning.
It goes on to say:
Of those aware of the latest budget, most (58 per cent) said it will not
strengthen the economy, while only 18 per cent (said) it will help Canada's
economic picture.
My question for the Hon. Member is: Knowing how much she respects polls, does she agree with this poll?
April 3, 1987

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I know there is the opportunity in this House many times to take cheap shots at Members across the floor, but I think that that is a particularly cheap one. You have obviously misinterpreted my position-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame on you!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-misinterpreted my position and my philosophy, which is not one based on polls but one based on consulting my constituents. I try to ensure that I, as their representative, understand and reflect their views.
While my colleague may view the Budget one way, I can only say that, in my area of the country, having discussed it with a great cross-section of people, it has been well received.
The people asked this Government to get the country's financial affairs in order, to bring down the deficit, and to manage the economy in a conservative and thoughtful manner.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Conservative!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what this Government is doing, and it is the first time in decades that it has been done. This Government is looking after the pennies, after the dollars. It is looking after the taxpayers' dollars. That is what this Government has done for the last two and a half years, and that is what this Government will continue to do for the next decade, and the next decade, and the next decade after that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on the Conservative Budget. Everybody knows the Conservative Government is always bragging about reducing the deficit. In the twenty minutes I am allowed, I will try to show there has been no reduction in the deficit at all.
Madam Speaker, between 1984-85 and 1987-88-three fiscal years-total Government revenue from income taxe increased by $22.3 billion. This means that during the period, the Government took $22.3 billion out of the taxpayers' pockets and now at the end of fiscal 1986-87, everybody agrees we will have a deficit of $32 billion, the same deficit we had during the fiscal year ending March 31, 1984, which was the last full fiscal year under a Liberal Government.
So after collecting $22.3 billion in taxes from Canadians, we still have the same deficit. That is the good management this Conservative Government promised us and promised Canadians in the fall of 1984.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It took them three years to do what the Liberals did in one.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And now, after three years, the results are there. The figures are there. We can prove that after three years, despite the fact they collected $22.3 billion, the deficit is still at the same level it was three years ago.
Of course, Conservative Members are going to say: That is what the Liberals say. Madam Speaker, it was our initial
The Budget-Mr. Gagliano
reaction when the Budget was brought down, but this week, we read comments by the C.D. Howe Institute which is after all an authority on economic affairs, and it had the following to say about the deficit, and I quote:
The year over year reductions are sizeable. They are not, however, as sizeable as they appear at first glance. The $2.42 billion reduction in fiscal year 1986-87 was made possible only by the last minute sale of Teleglobe Canada for $450 million and by the delaying of $700 million in special assistance to grain farmers until after March 31, 1987.
The Government reserved its neatest gimmick for fiscal year 1987-88, however, when it will gain $1.2 billion in additional revenue by accelerating remittance of source deductions of income tax, pension, and unemployment insurance premiums.
In the face of the increasing difficulty of maintaining the appearance of a downward deficit track, the Government has resorted to asset sales and fiscal tricks to fulfil its principle. This is not the way to reduce the underlying imbalance between spending and revenue. It is merely a way to finance it. The ongoing budget deficit appears to be stuck at over $30 billion.

Madam Speaker, this clearly and accurately says the Minister of Finance manipulates the tax data of his Government so that every year, he can come before the House and tell us that the deficit will again be less than $30 billion. Last year he did the same thing. And now the deficit is $32 billion. This year, he did the same, and considering the measures he took to bring the deficit down to less than $30 billion, the experts were already saying one month later that he would not achieve that objective and that the deficit would again be over $30 billion.
Madam Speaker, we all know that $22.3 billion were taken out of taxpayers' pockets through personal income tax and also quite a bit through federal sales tax. I should like to recall the remarks the Minister of Finance made about the federal sales tax in his Budget presentation, and I quote: "The federal sales tax is unfair and inefficient. It is a silent killer of jobs. It levies a higher tax-on average, one-third higher-on domestic manufacturers than on competing imports. This leads to plant closures and lost Canadian jobs. The base is narrow and similar goods can have very different burdens of tax. The sales tax is coming under increasing pressure and reform is increasingly urgent."
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance keeps repeating that the federal sales tax must be changed, that it is an unfair tax, yet again this year he did not bat an eye when he raised the federal sales tax on gas, and he also extended the federal sales tax to ice cream, candies and other snack foods which are bought and eaten by kids mostly. Then he raised the air transportation tax. Well now, if indeed the Minister is convinced that the federal sales tax is unfair and that a tax

April 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Gagliano
reform is urgent, why has he been keeping us waiting for a year and a half-for almost two years now-before delivering the goods, Madam Speaker?
This afternoon we listened to the two Conservative Members who spoke in this Budget debate, and they said over and over again that time has come for tax reform, that when we do get this tax reform they will reduce personal income tax, lower the federal sales tax, and so on. But we have been waiting for two and a half years, so what prevents the Conservative Government from going ahead with the tax reform, and in the meantime we would not be debating this proposed tax reform and Canadians would get some tax relief? Madam Speaker, taxes have been going up at a rate unprecedented since World War II.
I should like also to refer to a poll taken by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business among its members. This pool revealed two things. First, that businessmen for their tax burden is their main problem, the second being, red tape, all many forms they have to fill out every year for the avowed purpose of providing the Government with tax data. In order to get $1.2 billion from businesses, the Government is asking them to send those forms every fortnight instead of every month. By this single action, Madam Speaker, the Government doubles their paperwork businessmen just to meet the request of the Minister of Finance, because they are not required only to issue a cheque every two weeks, but to balance their books, fill out forms and send them to the Government. Since coming to power, the Government has not only imposed a greater tax burden, but increased significantly the amount of red tape, while advocating the opposite.
Madam Speaker, this Government is committed to a tax reform. When are we going to get it? I am wondering, because each time the Minister of Finance makes a speech, he keeps postponing its presentation. Let us say that we will get it eventually. He has promised a White Paper to inform the Canadian people of the Government's intention. We hope to get this document as soon as possible, so that we can comment on it and hear what Canadians from different walks of life have to say about the proposed new tax system.
There have been tax reforms in Canada before. Unfortunately, once the tax reform, was in place, there was twice as much red tape. If, therefore, the Minister of Finance wants to succeed in his endeavour, he must be clear and definite in his intention not to increase taxes. Such a tax reform should not be an excuse for the Government to get additional funds from Canadian taxpayers. They are already overtaxed. The purpose of this reform is to implement in Canada a simple, adequate and equitable tax system for all Canadians, no matter their social status. It is very important, therefore, that the Minister of Finance, when tabling his White Paper on tax reform, should take into account the need for fairness, so that the tax reform may be accepted and successful in Canada. Otherwise, this will be an exercise is futility. There will be new tax increases, nobody will be able to understand the income tax
legislation, and the economic development will stall because of our foolish habit of always increasing the tax burden.
Of course, we are not debating the tax reform this afternoon because we do not know yet what are the intentions of the Government nor the directions in which they intend to lead us in that regard. We are only hypothesizing about what the various ministers, and particularly the Finance Minister, indicated in their speeches across the country or during the Budget debate. So, we are anxious to learn what are the intentions of the Government and then, of course, as the Finance Minister requested, we will reply positively and suggest solutions to make our tax system fair and equitable.
Let us go back to the Budget, Madam Speaker. We have a very important tourist industry in Canada. Yet, once more in this Budget, we increase the tax on gas. I would like to quote a few paragraphs of a paper the Canadian Automobile Association issued in March 1987.
The 2.5 million member, not-for- profit Canadian Automobile Association takes this opportunity to present the views of its members on the fiscal policy affecting motorists and the travelling public as amended by the February, 1987 Budget presented by the federal Finance Minister, Michael Wilson.
Motorists are struggling with excessive taxes. Judging from the hundreds of thousands of submissions made last year to the Prime Minister, the Finance Minister and Members of Parliament, our 2.5 million members are extremely concerned and frustrated. They feel they have been overtaxed by more than $10 billion from 1981 to 1985 following the introduction of the National Energy Program and its various forms of taxes and special charges. Motorists are upset further with the current fixed rate of 5.5 cents per litre of excise tax which, compared to 1.5 cents per litre in August, 1985, represents more than a 250 per cent increase.
[ Translation]
As we can conclude from that document, Madam Speaker, Canadians are frustrated, exasperated, fed up with tax increases.
Madame Speaker, we all drive cars. Therefore, a 1 per cent increase in the sales tax on gas affects each and every one of us. We have certainly reached the point where enough is enough and we must find a way of reducing the tax burden.
My Conservative colleagues, Madam Speaker, praise the Budget as a good one. I would like to quote only a few newspaper reports that were published immediately following the Budget. On February 19, 1987, La Presse titled: "A $1.2 billion sleight of hand".

New bookkeeping makes govt, look S1.2B better.
That is a headline from The Ottawa Citizen.

"The Conservatives make individuals pay." "Ottawa takes less from businesses and more from individuals.", La Presse of February 19. "Business sectors are disappointed.", the same paper on the same day.
April 3, 1987



Quebec may sue over transfer payments-
That is the headline in The Gazette, Montreal.
"Great disappointment", Le Droit, February 1987.
Madam Speaker, these were the headlines of the major papers the day after the Budget, that empty document which used means I would call not exactly Kosher to bring the deficit below $30 billion. That is what the Conservative Government has done, a Government which has kept talking endlessly about fiscal responsibility. That is what the Minister of Finance has done, when he should be giving leadership to this country. When you introduce a budget, or financial statements, you must stick to the facts and not try to manipulate the figures to make people believe that the deficit is lower than it really is. That is the Budget, Madam Speaker, the third Conservative Budget. They want us to believe that they reduced the deficit, but it is still the same.
Madam Speaker, I would like to quote a few figures which show the impact of this Budget on Canadian families. Let us take, for example, a married couple with two children, where both parents work. In 1986, before the Budget, they had to pay $235 more in taxes. Before the February 1987 Budget they had a $400 increase, and now, after the 1987 Budget, they will have to pay $470 more.
Madam Speaker, here is another example, a married couple with two children, where both parents work, with an income of $30,000; in 1986 they paid $500, they had an increase of $590. In 1987, but before the February 1987 Budget, an increase of $875, and after the Budget it was $966 more. Madam Speaker, I say in 1987, before the February 1987 Budget, because we now have, each year, automatic increases, thanks to the May 1985 Conservative Budget which created a 3 per cent tax increase. We could	go on and	look at all theseincreases.	But it is enough	to look at	families,	MadamSpeaker, because that is were the main difference is, that is were we see the gap between rich and poor, a gap widened by the Government. A family with a $100,000 income had an increase, in 1986, of only $680. Their increase before the 1987 Budget was $1,145 and after the Budget, $2,285. It is obvious, Madam Speaker, that over the past three years the Conservative Government has not reduced the deficit. On March 31, 1984, the	deficit stood at $33	billion. On	March 31	1987, itstill stood	at $33 billion. Yet,	at the same	time, the	Government collected more than $20 billion in income tax from individuals.
This situation resulted in a widening of the gap between rich and poor. The poorer you are, the more income tax you pay; the richer you are, the less tax you pay.
Therefore, Madam Speaker, this social injustice is inacceptable to Canadians. The polls do prove it. I do hope that the fiscal reform will correct this situation.
The Budget-Mr. Gagliano

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have listened carefully to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-

speechtext: -d'Anjou!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture

speechtext:
-d'Anjou-I stand corrected-and 1 might like to make a few comments and ask him a question.
Firstly, my colleague mentionned the price of gasoline and the fact that the Canadian people had to pay a one cent increase. 1 want to remind him that, before the Conservatives come to power in 1984, the Liberals had introduced the National Energy Program. The Member did mention it in his speech a while ago, and I wish to remind him that in the period from 1981 to 1985, his party was in power, and it is his government that introduced a national energy program, which became our responsibility upon being elected. It was abolished. It was abolished because it was 105 per cent of the international price.
When we were elected, Madam Speaker, in 1984, gas was 60 cents a litre. Today, two and half years later, it is 52 cents. So we are still 8 cents lower. When the Liberals got elected in 1979-80, they promised they would fight us on the 18 cents increase. There was an increase of over a dollar a gallon under their government.
Madam Speaker, in all honesty, if the member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou is speaking for Canadian taxpayers, he should recognize that the father of the federal deficit is his own leader sitting there up front, that the true father of the federal deficit, the one who got Canadians into serious economic trouble, is his own leader. Indeed, Madam Speaker, when the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou extols the virtues of his party concerning poverty and concerning the gap between the rich and the poor, I will simply remind him that it was his government that allowed the highest salaried Canadians to get by without paying any taxes because of their tax shelters. Our government, our Minister of Finance, took responsible action in establishing a minimum tax, carving up tax shelters and seeing to it that the richest Canadians would have to pay taxes.
Madam Speaker, I would like to ask him whether it is our present Minister of Finance or the then Minister of Finance who is now his leader, that showed a greater sense of morality when our Minister of Finance set up a fair tax system and took steps to protect the poor against the rich while his own leader, the leader of the Opposition, as Minister of Finance, was doing everything he could to maintain the tax shelters benefiting the rich rather than the poor.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I shall be pleased to reply to the comments made by my Conservative colleague. Let us see first of all the energy issue. As for the price of gas which has gone from 60 cents a litre down to 49 cents, I certainly hope the members opposite will not try to take the credit for

April 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Gagliano
the oil price decrease because it is due to the international market.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is due to the energy policy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You say it is due to the energy policy. We will get back to the energy policy later on, but allow me to tell you that if the gas price has gone down in last few years, it is not because of the Conservatives, but mostly because the international price for crude oil has gone down. So do not take Canadian people . . . That's it, you look like manipulators; you are always taking credit for everything even though you don't deserve it. If the price of oil has decreased, it is not because of the Conservative policies, but indeed because of the international price for crude oil.
Now let us get back to the energy policy. I would like to ask my colleague if he knows how many Canadians, controlled the industry when the Liberal government introduced the National Energy Program. Almost none. Today, more than 50 per cent of the Canadian energy industry is controlled by Canadians, not by foreigners. Look at the facts. Do not focus only on the negative side of the NEP. Consider the positive side also, and ask Canadians whether, in pre-NEP days, the energy industry in Canada was not indeed totally controlled by Americans. Ask that to Canadians, and see what they will say.
Now, Madam Speaker, he asks me who is the fairer between the Minister of Finance and my leader. I want to remind my colleague that the present Minister of Finance is the one who de-indexed old age pensions. Let us remember Mrs. Denis and her famous Charlie Brown, and I hope he is listening to us and will remember too ... It is precisely my leader who introduced that protection, who granted to Canadians, especially to the elderly, to the low income people that protection against inflation. Therefore, 1 obviously choose my leader, Madam Speaker.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is always easy to make a point as the Hon. Member just did when he mentioned indexing, but as usual, you too forgot that time when the increase in the cost of living index was 12 per cent and that indexing was frozen at 5 and 6 per cent. Because you too only mention whatever suits you not only because your present leader, who was Minister of Finance at the time, the father of the Canadian deficit, managed to turn a surplus into a deficit, which is quite a feat, and your finance critic as well, who is responsible for deficits at the provincial level. In view of his record at the provincial level, he was brought in at the federal level to see if he could do any better. All your Finance Ministers, be they MacEachen, Turner, Lalonde, Chretien have all introduced budgets that were called by the name of their authors, and they were all responsible for our deficit.
All the economists of the time have called them disasters one after the other. I hope you will remember that. You were not in politics at that time, but I suppose you read the papers once in a while about it. I was surprised to hear what you said earlier. Here is my question. A moment ago, you spoke about
the poor contractors who are overwhelmed by tax burden, red tape and the fact that they now have to complete and return forms twice a month, to pay whatever tax they owe to the Federal Government. Through a housekeeping measure which is commendable, I think, we will be able to recover tax payable to the Government. Those companies are big enough because it applies to amounts of $ 15 000 at least. I listened to your colleague for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) who keeps repeating that we are against low income Canadians and that we always give to the rich. As far as I can see, we have an advocate of the rich and you are the champion of business. Personally I would be tempted to ask what you have to say about interest rates, for example, because that is another element. You will undoubtedly reply that the federal Government does not have anything to do with that. And then for the first time the national deficit has been going down, for the first time public expenditures have declined, and this is something you were unable to accomplish over 20 years. This is the first time there is a net decrease since 1952, I think, since the Korean war. With current interest rates, people can renew their mortgages at 9 per cent, whereas when you were in office you had budgets, the Lalonde budget among others, where the deficit was expected to be in the $3-to-$4 billion range and finally ended up at the $15 billion level. Not to worry! Who cares! Never mind the expenses! We can spend freely, Canadians will pay. The children or the great grandchildren will pay for that.
We have shown the Canadian people that we were able to get a handle on the rising federal deficit and repair the mistakes you made over the years, so people regained confidence and interest rates went down. And the companies you are talking about, businessmen, what do you have to say about that and the interest rates? Do you not agree that companies are now investing heavily in Canada, that ours ranks first among industrialized countries in terms of projected investments, so what do you have to say about interest rates? Would you not agree that the present Minister of Finance has come up with policies which have driven interest rates down, a better performance than when you were on the Government side? Respond to that, please!

speechtext: Debate. The Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to speak on the Budget. As some of my colleagues have pointed out, it is an eminently forgettable Budget. It is what my mother would have called chip and porridge, a Budget with nothing good, it is just there. In this case, however, there is no porridge to go with it.
My fundamental criticism of the Budget is the implicit assumption underlying it that all is well with the Canadian federation and all we need is a bit more belt-tightening to get our deficit down and everything will then continue purring on just as though everything is wonderful. It is in fact a do-nothing Budget. Its myopic point of view ignores what is happening to hundreds of Canadian communities and the people who live in those communities.
I would like to share just a couple of examples to bring this home to members of the government Party. First, I would like to talk about the community of La Scie and the Baie Verte Peninsula in Newfoundland. A delegation from that community appeared before the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Oceans a few weeks ago. They pointed out that in the Baie Verte Peninsula since 1979 some 1,300 jobs have been lost. They depend very much on the fisheries plant there, and the entire inshore fishery has been neglected by the Department in favour of the offshore fishery which is controlled by two large companies, National Sea and Fisheries Products International. It is interesting that the latter company, having been established as a Crown corporation and given a good allocation of fish, has now become a profit-making venture and, being so, will now be privatized. In the meantime, in communities like La Scie who depend upon the inshore fishery, there are not enough fish allocated to the inshore fishery to maintain the fish plant there at anywhere near the level at which it should be. In 1979 the plant processed 29.6 million pounds of fish. Since that time there has been a continuous decline, and last year less than half that amount, only 13.3 million pounds, was processed. These people live in the very place where further allocations of cod are going to be taken from Newfoundland and given to France. That not only hurts them economically, it hurts them in the sense of feeling they belong to a nation that does not care for them as a community or as individuals.
The only other major source of employment in the area is an asbestos mine which itself has had a 74 per cent reduction in its workforce over the last few years. There is nothing being done for those people by the Government, either within the Department of Fisheries and Oceans or in the larger sense of eliminating disparity. For example, the NDP has called for a Northern Fisheries Development Corporation which would focus on the inshore fishery and help it to develop. However, we do not see anything like that kind of an initiative being taken by the federal Government.
The Budget should have addressed those kinds of issues. It should have addressed the issue of regional disparity. Again, the NDP has made suggestions which the Government chooses not to accept. We suggested there should have been a $815 million community initiatives fund and a $200 million single industry community diversification fund. Things like that would help a community like La Scie and hundreds of others across Canada to develop alternative employment.
It is interesting that the official unemployment rate in Newfoundland today is 19.2 per cent. However, Earl McCurdy, the Vice-President of the Fishermen's Union of Newfoundland, has pointed out that if the people of that province had the same rate of participation in the labour force as they have in Ontario, then the actual unemployment rate in Newfoundland would be a staggering 38 per cent. That is the situation in Newfoundland.
The other community I would like to talk about is in my own constituency, and that is Cowichan Valley. It has been hard hit by changes in the forest industry over the last few years. Several large mills have closed, and others have drastically reduced their workforce due to technological change. The same sort of thing is happening in the logging industry. Fewer workers are getting out more wood. We are continuing to export raw logs overseas.
The situation has resulted in many older workers being laid off. Who wants to hire a worker of 45, 50 or 55 years of age whose skills are all in one industry? They have literally nowhere to go. I have had people like that come into my office looking for some kind of assistance to help them continue to lead productive lives. These are people who are used to working, used to paying their own way. Suddenly they find that they have no jobs and no prospect of jobs. I know I am not the only Member of Parliament who has experienced that. I see one of the Hon. Members from Prince George here and I know he has had the same kind of experience. Other older workers have had the experience of being bumped down in seniority and have ended up doing the kinds of jobs which have traditionally been done by much younger workers. They are required to do heavy physical work, which may be suitable to younger workers, but not to people in their age bracket.
There is also the situation of younger workers who cannot get their first job in their home community. They are forced to leave home and look for work elsewhere. We do not want to build a Canada in which people have to leave home in order to find work. We want a Canada where people can build their lives in the communities where their families are. The real unemployment rate in the Cowichan Valley is around 30 per cent. In the last week in British Columbia we have seen the closure of Unemployed Action Centres which have tried to provide some help to the people about whom I have just been talking who have been caught by this terrible downturn in the economy.
April 3, 1987

The Canada Jobs Strategy has recently designated the Cowichan Valley for the Community Futures Program. We are glad to have that designation, but I want to emphasize that unless there are are other government initiatives which affect the entire economy of the Province of British Columbia this Community Futures Program will not be able to address the crying need for jobs in the Cowichan Valley. That goes for other communities in British Columbia which have been designated as well. We need a global package which will get the entire community going.
I was interested to hear the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) speak about the decline in employment following Expo. Of course many of us had been saying all along that the jobs at Expo were short-term jobs. The Government is using the fact that they were short-term jobs as an excuse for the very high rate of unemployment in British Columbia right now. She expects that these people will soon drop off the unemployment rolls and that that will bring the unemployment statistics down. Of course it will bring the statistics down, but it will not do a damn thing about the fact that these people would really like to have jobs. It is simply the way in which the Government keeps statistics. I apologize for the language, Madam Speaker, but the people in British Columbia feel very strongly about this.
The estimates on the need for a forestry program in British Columbia vary, but most experts agree that the cost of an effective program of reforestation ranges between $200 million and $300 million per year. This figure would cover the cost of replanting not satisfactorily restocked lands and replacing what is cut annually, as well as providing some funding for intensive forestry. Contrast the $200 million to $300 million needed annually with the money available under the economic development agreement signed by the federal Government and the Province of British Columbia. The federal Government is contributing a total of $150 million over five years, or $30 million per year, which will be matched by the province for a total of $60 million which is less than one-quarter of the funds needed to do an effective job of reforestation.
A recent report put out by the University of British Columbia authored by Sten Nilsson on forest economics points out that British Columbia is only 15 years away from economic catastrophe unless we do something about our forest resources. Seventeen thousand direct jobs have already been lost and a further 7,000 jobs are about to be lost unless we take action. We have not yet seen that action. I pointed out a few weeks ago that only 48 per cent of the professional foresters who have graduated from UBC in the last six years have been able to find jobs in their field. Twenty-one per cent are still completely unemployed. We are training people but do not provide the jobs for them even though everyone recognizes that there is a crying need for forestry in British Columbia.
What is the matter with the Government that it cannot bring together the skills and resources to meet the needs? The needs are there and recognized. The resources and skills are there. Yet, only 48 per cent of our professional foresters can
The Budget-Mr. Manly
find jobs after they have graduated and the others have to go and whistle. There is something wrong, and the fault lies with the Government and its failure to address this kind of situation adequately.
There are in fact, Madam Speaker, two economies developing in Canada, one for central Canada and one for the region. Yesterday in British Columbia there was new labour legislation introduced which will make British Columbia's economy more of a third world economy by weakening the rights of workers to organize and fight for better conditions.
The neglect of our resource economy by the Government is a major indictment of it. It has failed. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was campaigning he promised that there would be a separate department of forestry. He recognized the need for a separate department with its own budget, its own employees, and a full-time Minister. Instead, we have a junior Minister who reports to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and shares forestry with mining. The people in the mining sector are probably very concerned that they do not have more clout in Cabinet as well. However, for our number one industry across Canada to have only a Minister of State reporting to the Minister of Agriculture is criminal. We neglected the primary wealth producers and the regions wherein that primary wealth is being produced.
With regard to the situation of fishermen, there has been a doubling of licence fees on the Pacific Coast and an increase in wharfage fees for both fishing and pleasure boats. That will deal a blow to our tourism industry as well. There has been no permanent funding for the Salmonid Enhancement Program. Representatives from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans appeared before the committee and pointed out that in order to do an adequate job of maintaining small craft harbours they needed $120 a year. They are getting $48 million a year. Unless further money is allocated within five years the Government will have to close down 150 Class C harbours across Canada. That will mean shutting down the basic infrastructure of our Atlantic and Pacific coasts in many communities which depend upon those harbours.
The Government claims that there are are too many people in the fishing industry. Its slogan is, too many fishermen taking too few fish. Yet, the Government is doing nothing to create alternative employment. Canada did not become a nation by relying on market forces. If we wanted to rely on market forces we would have joined the United States a long time ago. Canada became a nation because we had a vision of a nation which would extend from sea to sea and a Government which was prepared to work for that. Right now we have a Government that is prepared to allow the market to determine what happens. As a result, we have seen that in the last year all but 5,000 of the 137,000 jobs that have been created were in the Province of Ontario.
Is it too much for provinces like Newfoundland and British Columbia to have expected that a federal Budget would have

April 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Manly
recognized their problems and taken action? Is not a Budget supposed to be a process by which the Government looks at all of our resources and our needs and tries to bring the two into balance?
We must question the priorities of the Government. Are native self-government and settlement of land claims too expensive, as the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) has claimed, or does the Government simply have its priorities wrong? Does the Government have no alternative to the Budget which does no more than apologize for regional disparity?
The fact is that spending on economic and regional development in this fiscal year which just began will be about $3 billion less than when the Conservative Government was elected in 1984. Regional disparity has increased and less money is being spent to try to overcome that.
Earlier Conservative Budgets have loaded huge tax increases on the backs of individual Canadians, particularly Canadians in low and middle-income tax brackets. At the same time, they offered upper-income Canadians more tax loopholes like the $500,000 capital gains tax. The Budget continues that trend.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised tax reform during the 1984 election campaign. It is another promise that has been postponed, and now we are supposed to see something in upcoming months. Perhaps the Government could explain to Canadians why an increase in tax could be slapped on at midnight of budget day, but it is a different story when it comes to tax reform that might give them a break.
Of course, Canadians should be concerned about what might be in that tax reform because there are many rumours that while there might be a slight decrease in the income tax rate it will be balanced by a business transfer tax. The rumours are that there are to be no exemptions to that business transfer tax, which will mean an increased cost on food and other basic necessities. It is the kind of tax that is once again most regressive and will hit the poor people of this country the hardest.
I suggest there are some measures the Government can implement that would begin to introduce some fairness into the tax system. First, it should eliminate the $500,000 lifetime capital gains tax exemption. This measure will cost over $1 billion by the end of this year. The exemption benefits only the rich. In 1983, only 10 per cent of taxpayers who had less than $40,000 income could claim an average capital gain of $1,000. Elowever, 61 per cent of taxpayers who had more than $250,000 income claimed an average capital gain of $57,461. Of course, we believe the capital gains exemption should remain for principal dwellings, family farms, fishermen or small businesses that have been built up in a family for a period of years.
We believe the Government should tighten up on the minimum tax. It should use the revenues from a fair taxation of capital gains to restore the basic federal tax exemption. We
want it to put a halt to personal and sales tax increases for ordinary Canadians.
By 1990, individual Canadians will have been hit by a $35 billion tax increase by the Conservatives, while at the same time only $128 million will have been slapped onto the corporations. That represents only 1 per cent of the over-all tax increase. Is that fair?
I have a number of other comments but you are indicating that my time is up. I look forward to answering perhaps some questions on these issues.
