speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to make a couple of comments on the Hon. Member's speech. First, he mentioned two specific communities in Newfoundland, Baie Verte and La Scie. He said there has been a decrease in employment in the Baie Verte asbestos mine. The original owners of that mine closed it down because of a lack of market and the protest from around the world by environmentalists and others about the potential health hazard of asbestos. If it were not for the fact that the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland put some $18 million into the asbestos mine in Baie Verte, there would be much higher unemployment there today. I doubt very much if the mine would even be operating.
The Hon. Member also spoke about inshore fishermen in La Scie. Obviously Mr. McCurdy of the Fishermen's Union could not have filled him in , and I am sure the Hon. Member would not have Members of the House believing that the Government of Canada is doing nothing for the fishermen of La Scie and other places in Newfoundland.
The fact is that the Hon. Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) recently issued a shrimp licence to a company so that it could land the shrimp in La Scie and provide decent employment there. Furthermore, for the Hon. Member's information, for at least three or four years the inshore fishermen of Newfoundland have not been able to catch the inshore fish allocations that presently exist. Whether that is because of water temperatures or ice conditions that prevent them from getting out when the fish could be caught, I cannot say. Apparently it is not even evident to the scientists and biologists who are doing research in that area. I might say that they are doing extra research from St. John's, Newfoundland because the Minister has increased the number of employees in the scientific branch in the Department of Fisheries and Oceans in Newfoundland.
I suggest that the Hon. Member check his source of information to determine whether there is indeed a community Futures Program in existence in Baie Verte. While I do not want to say there is and perhaps mislead the House, I am pretty damn sure, to use the Member's words, that there is such a program. I would not want him to leave the House with any misunderstanding.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. He comes from a part of Newfoundland that is very
April 3, 1987

dependent upon the fishing industry. He knows the difficulties that the people of Newfoundland are facing there.
The dependence of the Baie Verte Peninsula on the asbestos mine should be of concern to all of us because asbestos mining does pose health hazards. The fact that they do not have any alternative except to engage in an industry which has very high risks for people who work in it should be a real cause of concern for all Members of the House.
We become concerned when there is a building that has asbestos insulation that is covered with panelling. We say that that creates a hazard. Yet we expect people will work in those mines, and we have to be concerned about that. I can understand how people who have no other source of employment would see that as being something that is better than having no other means of making a livelihood. Yet it is a terrible price to pay. I am sure the Hon. Member will agree with that.
The Hon. Member pointed out that the Minister has just granted a shrimp allocation to the community of La Scie. That could be, and I think it is good. The basic fact is that there was a delegation from La Scie which appeared before the Fisheries Committee. Members of that delegation made a very moving and eloquent plea for their region. They asked that there be a further allocation of fish which could be treated at the plant at La Scie. I certainly support that. If the Government has other programs which could ameliorate somewhat the situation in La Scie and Baie Verte, the more power to it. But the fact remains that the Government and this Budget have not done enough for the people of Newfoundland, a province where there is an unemployment rate running as high as 38 per cent, especially when we consider the number of people who want to work and cannot. I am sure the Hon. Member would be the last person to get up in this Chamber and say that he thinks the Government is doing an adequate job for the people of Newfoundland. I am sure the Hon. Member has some time left and that he would not want to get up and make that type of an assertion.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yes, I would want to say that I will never be satisfied until there is no unemployment in Newfoundland. In fact, I would be very proud if I had to pass out invitations to other Members telling them that there is work available in Newfoundland because there are not enough labourers and because there is full employment. I would be very proud of that.
What I was trying to say is that it is wrong to give the impression that the Government does not care about the people of Newfoundland, or the people of any other part of the country for that matter. All 1 was trying to point out is that the mine in Baie Verte would have been closed if it were not for the assistance it has received from the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland.
I was also trying to point out the effort of trying to put in place additional work in La Scie through the giving of a
The Budget-Mr. Manly
shrimp allocation. I could have gone further and said that last year there were supplementary crab licences issued in order to create additional work. But the Hon. Member knows that it would be irresponsible for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) to issue additional fish allocations to anyone from the offshore sector if it is not appropriate under the guidelines of the scientific evidence on which he has to make his decisions.
I can also tell the Hon. Member that there have been efforts made in terms of the revitalization of the sealing industry with the location of a plant in Fleur de Lys which is also on the Baie Verte peninsula. Federal and provincial money has gone into that effort. So the Government is trying, but as the Hon. Member knows, Newfoundland is not a manufacturing area. There is only certain potential for the resources that we have to create as much employment as we possibly can. I would certainly like to see less unemployment. I am sure my colleagues would like to hear suggestions from anyone who might be able to enhance employment in Newfoundland.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, if the Government really cared it would not be allocating fish to France in that area. It would have had some policies that would have seen that out of 137,000 jobs created last year more than 5,000 of them would have gone to some other province than Ontario.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am delighted this afternoon to rise in the House to share with you and through you with my colleagues and my constituents some of my thoughts about the 1987 Budget which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) presented. It is a Budget which really brought good news for Canadians. The budget experience this year was an unusual one for me. I would like to share it with you, Madam Speaker.
I live in and represent the federal riding of Nepean- Carleton which is in so many ways a microcosm of this great country in which we have the privilege of living. It is a large riding from a population point of view, while being an excellent mixture of urban and rural people. It represents an excellent mixture of entrepreneurship and people involved in small business, people who are involved in the high technology business, people who are involved in dairy production and so on. One of the most striking things about this community is its vibrancy and its growth. When we look at the community today we see that there are about 1,900 small businesses in it. I ask Hon. Members to think of what that translates into in terms of jobs, in terms of the creation of new wealth and in terms of the enjoyment of life. Those 1,900 small businesses, together with some of the other features of the community, translate into about 36,000 or 37,000 jobs. These jobs are filled by people who come to work into the riding every morning who have a positive work experience during the day. This community is really a thriving business community.
What have these businessmen, these farm producers and dairy producers to say to me about the economic world in which they would like to operate? Their consistent message to

April 3, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Tupper
me is simple. They say: "We would like the Government to get out of our hair, to simplify the regulations and the guidelines under which we must work". The second thing they say to me is: "We want to stay on a steady path. We want to know what the goals of the Government are so that we can work side by side with those regulations without having our goals move from year by year by year. In this way we can have a constant business plan, a constant goal, a constant level of productivity and a constant level of exports for which we can aim".
The unique budget experience for me this year boiled down to how few calls of a negative nature I received from my constituents with respect to the Budget. How few were they? 1 would like to share with Members of the House the fact that I received more negative calls when Petro-Canada, Esso and Texaco upped the price of gasoline by two cents or three cents a litre when they should have only done it by one cent a litre. In fact, most of the calls I had about the Budget were thank you's or calls of a congratulatory nature. The small businesspersons and members of the farm community who called me said: "Thank you for leaving the half-a-million-dollar capital gains exemption in place on an ongoing basis". They said: "Thank you from the high technology community for removing the import duties on many of the components that we have to bring into the riding in order to add value to them in the process of manufacturing and which we then export". 1 was thanked by the booksellers and the book retail people in my riding who simply said: "Thank you for removing the tariffs on the importation of books which were such an impediment". This community, under the fiscal regime of which we are now a part, is growing. It is buoyant.
By way of example, this morning I was out at the sodturning ceremony for a new high school, a high school that the City of Kanata and the Carleton Board of Education are building together, the core of which in fact is going to be used jointly by the community and the Board of Education, for the over-all betterment of the young people and people of all ages in that community.
To take and build on that, over the last two and a half years, economic growth and job creation in Canada has exceeded that of all other major industrial countries. The Government has worked hard to attain this progress. We have made tough decisions, and we have applied firm and disciplined management to all sections of the Canadian economy.
It should be noted that these results have been achieved in the face of a world economy that has become not only more competitive, but also more uncertain and more volatile.
Going back some 30 months, or to mid-1984, when we had the privilege of forming the Government of Canada, we had just gone through 15 consecutive years in which the federal deficit had increased annually. By then, it had increased to some $38 billion. When one translates that into what it means per person or per household in Canada, it translates into $23,000 per household across this great nation of ours. Just
think of that! You and 1, and everyone across Canada, because of what the Government had been doing on our behalf, had a debt of $23,000.
In November of 1984, against that background, faced with disturbing trends, trends that posed a threat to sustained economic growth, permanent jobs, and greater opportunities for Canadians, the Government's renewal strategy began.
The agenda for economic renewal set out the Government's philosophy of economic management and its blueprint for the renewal of the Canadian economy.
That meant, Madam Speaker, adopting policies that helped small business, policies that fostered entrepreneurship and risk taking, policies that promoted innovation and created a positive climate for the growth and expansion of new enterprises. It meant making the Canadian economy more dynamic, more flexible, and more competitive, so that companies, small and large, high technology companies such as those located in my constituency, can thrive and compete in world markets.
That was the challenge. We started a program of economic renewal, and we are continuing down the road of growth, of job creation, and of economic vitality.
Given our economic successes over the past 30 or 32 months, Canadians have every reason to be encouraged about their future.
The Government has made good progress in delivering on its fiscal commitment. The deficit is down from some $38.3 billion in 1984-85, to $32 billion last year, and projections indicate a further decline to some $29 billion in the fiscal year just beginning.
This is an over-all decline of some 23 to 24 per cent. Through dealing positively with the deficit, the Government is ensuring that the well-being of all Canadians is preserved; that the future of my children and my grandchildren, and yours, will be such that they will have a much more creative environment in which to grow and to develop and to prosper.
We are determined to provide that opportunity for all Canadians, an opportunity that is not burdened by debt. The Government has acted across a full range of its programs and operations to implement the fundamental requirements of economic renewal. As a result, Canadians now have an economic climate that encourages private initiative and rewards success. It is starting to pay tremendous dividends for us.
The real growth of Canada's economy has averaged about 3.5 per cent per year, second only to Japan and much stronger than that of the United States. Consumer confidence has risen sharply and is at an all time high. Spending by consumers has provided a major impetus to growth.
Across this land, 705,000 new jobs have been created. Our employment growth has been stronger than that of any other major industrial country. The employment rate has dropped by some 2.1 per cent; short-term interest rates are at the lowest levels in over a decade, perhaps some 14 years; mortgage rates
April 3, 1987

have fallen by more than 3 per cent, making home ownership a possibility for all young Canadians; inflation is in the area of 4 per cent.
I invite you to translate those figures into the stability and the economic activity that can result.
In the agricultural sector, the farmers of my constituency welcome the fact that we did not change the capital gains tax. They are pleased with the fact that when we increased the excise tax on motor gasoline and diesel fuel- by one cent per litre, we at the same time increased the rebate in a matching way.
One thing that has, in large part, gone unnoticed in the Budget is the fact that we announced that mobile veterinary clinics could come into Canada on a duty-free basis- something that was not possible before the Budget. This type of mobile veterinary clinic is not manufactured in Canada. This measure will be of extraordinary value to the agricultural community.
The small business and high technology communities of Canada welcomed the announcement of the removal of tariff measures on a number of import products. Specifically, the Budget restored duty-free entry for computer parts, semiconductors, and books. As far as the high technology community is concerned, a community which, in so many ways, is involved with a value-added type of activity, these measures may result in increased profits by as much as 50 per cent.
Not all countries, Madam Speaker, are as privileged as Canada, and one thing this Budget does is to give strong support to developing countries. Canada's foreign aid expenditures will be some $450 million higher than the 1984-85 level, an increase of some 21.8 per cent.
We are committed to achieving the objective of 0.5 per cent of our Gross National Product being allocated to official development assistance.
We have taken other measures to help developing countries. For example, we are providing all financial assistance now in the form of grants, instead of loans. As well, we now permit
The Budget-Mr. Tupper
duty-free access for a range of goods from Commonwealth Caribbean countries.
Let me turn for a moment, Madam Speaker, to the mining sector. While it may surprise you to hear me speak of the mining sector this afternoon, I have had an enormous amount of input from that sector complimenting this Government and the Finance Minister for maintaining the flow-through share arrangement for our mineral resource industry, an industry that is so vital to Canada. It is an industry that contributes a great deal to our exports and hence to our foreign currency position. There are some 65 mining communities scattered across Canada, from Newfoundland to British Columbia.
Last year, we spent some $550 million on mineral exploration in Canada. Of that amount, some $400 million-$264 million on the part of the junior mining companies and some $136 million by the seniors-was spent through the flowthrough share arrangement.
In other words, Madam Speaker, about 73 per cent of the funds raised for mineral exploration in Canada last year were funds that came through the flow-through share arrangements, giving some indication of how important that program is. I want to compliment the Finance Minister for ensuring that that mechanism stays in place.
In closing, Madam Speaker, the Government has acted on initiatives of fundamental importance to the Canadian economy. We inherited a challenge, and we have met that challenge. We will continue moving forward with our program for economic renewal in a carefully managed and consistent way. Staying the course is the key to our future prosperity.
